The nutritional quality of food may matter more than how much it is processed, according to new research.

Researchers say products often categorised as processed, such as canned beans, plant-based dairy alternatives, or breakfast cereals fortified with essential vitamins, can still contribute to a healthy, balanced diet.

They added that advising the public to avoid all ultra-processed food (UPF) could inadvertently hinder dietary quality, as many "healthy" processed products such as whole grain bread and canned fruit can still be “beneficial”.

The findings are based on the analysis of data from more than 200,000 people across three large studies in the US. Participants had their dietary habits tracked over several decades, from the 1980s to the 2020s, and were grouped into four categories according to their plant-based eating habits.

These categories included healthy/ultra-processed, which included plant-based milk and yoghurts, and healthy/minimally processed, including fresh fruit and nuts.

Unhealthy/ultra-processed products included fast food and fizzy drinks, and unhealthy/minimally processed items included fruit juice, potatoes and white rice.

Some breakfast cereals fortified with vitamins can still contribute to a healthy diet, according to researchers ( PA )

Some 26,209 people went on to develop cardiovascular disease while around 21,000 developed type 2 diabetes and 55,493 died.

The study found that the risk of death, diabetes and cardiovascular disease varied depending on the overall quality of a person’s diet.

Those who ate more healthily had a lower risk, regardless of whether food was ultra-processed or minimally processed.

Xiaowen Wang, a postdoctoral research fellow in the department of nutrition at Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, said: “While many ultra-processed foods tend to be of poor nutritional quality and should generally be limited or avoided, processing itself is not inherently harmful.”

Ms Wang said the findings suggest that people should focus on what they are eating overall, not just if it is processed.

“A healthy plant-based diet rich in whole grains, fruits, vegetables, nuts, legumes and healthy plant oils is beneficial, even if it includes some processed foods,” she added.

“Advising people to universally ‘avoid ultra-processed foods’ can lead to lower diet quality since healthy ultra-processed foods are beneficial and unhealthy minimally processed foods are detrimental.

“People should prioritise the quality of foods rather than focusing solely on the level of processing. Aim for more nutrient-dense, high-quality foods to help lower your risk of chronic diseases.”

The findings will be presented at Nutrition 2026, the flagship meeting of the American Society for Nutrition, on July 28.

News.title: The Chelsea pensioners: Why Xabi Alonso has suddenly shifted transfer strategy to sign older players
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. England international? Tick. Premier League winner? Tick. At least 35 years old? Erm, tick that too. Chelsea’s transfer policy has taken a surprising turn this summer, ripped up and rewritten, and it’s led the club to the doors of Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck.

Chelsea are working on deals to add both to Xabi Alonso’s squad in time for the start of the new season. They have also missed out on other experienced targets such as John Stones, 32, who is set for a move to Inter Milan, and Granit Xhaka, 33, who Sunderland are determined to keep as captain.

It is a stunning departure from one of the most aggressive youth-focused transfer strategies in Premier League history, which has brought waves of potential to Stamford Bridge replete with lavish decade-long contracts. BlueCo have been dogmatic, signing only one player over 25 – defender Tosin Adarabioyo – since the summer of 2023. Last season, Chelsea signed 10 players ranging in age from 18 (Estevao, Kendry Paez) to 23 (Joao Pedro).

open image in gallery Danny Welbeck could be heading to Stamford Bridge ( Getty )

It would be wrong to say the transfer policy has been completely flawed. Nurturing young talent and investing in sellable assets is the modus operandi of many well-run clubs. Cole Palmer and Moises Caicedo were youthful signings, as were Enzo Fernandez and Wesley Fofana. Estevao and Joao Pedro had excellent debut seasons in an underwhelming Chelsea team.

But a 10th-placed finish in last season’s Premier League suggested something was fundamentally wrong. Chelsea picked up eight red cards along the way (Arsenal and Manchester City, the top two, didn’t receive any) and the lack of discipline hinted at a deep flaw in the mentality and behaviour of the squad.

The meek Champions League exit at the hands of Paris Saint-Germain was damning. Liam Rosenior’s team were heading towards a valuable 2-2 draw in Paris before a succession of needless individual errors saw them succumb to a 5-2 defeat, and winger Pedro Neto pushed over a ballboy in a show of ill-discipline. This reporter was at the second leg, when young defender Mamadou Sarr was thrown in at right-back and had a disastrous game as Chelsea wilted against Europe’s elite.

That last-16 exit would have fed into the club’s decision to recalibrate an inexperienced squad. The pursuit of older heads is a tacit admission that the talented squad BlueCo had built lacked leadership and proven quality. The recruitment of Xabi Alonso, a Bundesliga-winning manager, is in itself a marked change from the appointments of Rosenior and Enzo Maresca before him.

open image in gallery Cole Palmer looks disconsolate during Chelsea’s Champions League defeat by PSG ( PA )

Which is not to say that Chelsea have entirely abandoned their former transfer strategy. If anything, they’ve doubled down. Morgan Rogers, 24, has joined for an eye-watering £117m in a seven-year deal. Atalanta right-back Marco Palestra, 21, and Sporting winger Geovany Quenda, 19, have signed seven- and eight-year deals respectively. Welbeck may as well ask for a contract until he’s 44.

The Blues are still buying talented teenagers, like 17-year-old Kazakh striker Dastan Satpayev, who scored in Alonso’s first friendly against Western Sydney Wanderers in Australia on Tuesday.

Against that backdrop, it might seem a little clumsy, even naive, to simply bolt on vast experience to a young squad, rather than taking the time to mature players within the group. This season’s leaders could have been two players who started the World Cup final, Marc Cucurella and Enzo Fernandez, but one has gone to Real Madrid and the other – who was sent off – wants to leave.

The new strategy is a shift beyond proven players to players past their peak, entering the winter of their careers. Is this a piece of savvy business in the transfer market? Or an overreaction to redress an obvious imbalance? Chelsea supposedly chose Rogers’ £117m fee because it was £1m more than Manchester City paid for Elliot Anderson, which doesn’t scream boardroom maturity.

open image in gallery Jordan Henderson could soon be joining Chelsea ( Reuters )

A valid question remains about whether Chelsea have enough players in their prime. Alonso’s likely starting XI has only one outfield player over the age of 26 (Trevoh Chalobah is 27). Over the past four years the club have sold a number of players in or near their prime, such as Kai Havertz, Mateo Kovacic, Noni Madueke, Conor Gallagher and Mason Mount, a lucrative selling strategy causing a mid-20s talent drain.

And perhaps the most costly consequence of BlueCo’s reign is to the sense of what Chelsea are as a club, of who they are meant to be. Their Premier League dominance two decades ago was characterised by strong personalities who forged deep connections to Stamford Bridge. That sense of identity cannot be bought in the transfer market, whether you spend £117m on a 24-year-old or sign a veteran for free.

There is an argument that, in time, the work that has gone into recruiting some of the best teenagers in the world will eventually come to fruition, that those players now in their early 20s will be future leaders. But that involves time, and Chelsea managers don’t tend to get much of it.

open image in gallery Xabi Alonso directs from the touchline against Western Sydney Wanderers ( PA )

So Alonso must hope that his new recruits have an immediate impact. Henderson and Welbeck are known for bringing positive energy and professionalism to a squad. Both tend to be fit for most of the season, ironic considering Henderson is now recovering from a broken arm sustained falling over a hoarding. Welbeck’s career was hindered by injuries but he has transformed himself physically, making at least 36 appearances for Brighton in each of the past four seasons.

Alonso is not their only admirer. Thomas Tuchel strongly considered Welbeck for England’s World Cup squad, and was questioned over his decision to select Henderson. Perhaps his answers help to explain Chelsea’s thinking. “What Hendo brings to every team is leadership, character, personality, energy,” said Tuchel. “He is a serial winner … He is the glue in every team that he has played, the glue that makes things special.”

News.title: Chelsea in 10-goal thriller as ‘Alonso ball’ brings risk and reward
News.content:
Chelsea’s first match under the management of Xabi Alonso was a 10-goal thriller in Australia, as the Premier League side eventually showed their class in a 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers.

Star striker João Pedro, who was controversially left out of Brazil’s World Cup squad, scored a nine-minute hat-trick after coming off the bench with half an hour of the friendly remaining.

Alonso had selected a youthful team for the first hour before bringing nine senior players, including João Pedro, into the side in the second half. According to Transfermarkt, Chelsea’s squad is valued at over £1.3bn while their opponents a more modest £5.86m.

Teenage signing Dastan Satpayev, midfielder Dario Essugo and winger Jamie Gittens also found the net for Chelsea, who were defensively vulnerable for long spells for the game.

Here are five things Telegraph Sport learned from Alonso’s first match.

João Pedro picks up where he left off

João Pedro scored 13 goals in the second half of last season and his impressive performances resulted in the 24-year-old being named Chelsea’s player of the campaign. It was something of a surprise, then, when he was left out of Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil squad this summer.

The good news for Chelsea is that João Pedro’s absence from the World Cup has given him plenty of time to recover ahead of the new campaign, and he looked thrillingly sharp in his second-half performance against Western Sydney Wanderers. The difference in class between João Pedro and Liam Delap, the man he replaced, was clear for all to see.

Two of the Brazilian’s three goals were classy, composed finishes — and he also created a goal for Gittens after surging past three defenders on the left wing. João Pedro looks like he means business.

News.title: China’s chip breakthrough triggers global tech rout
News.content:
China has achieved a breakthrough in developing technology crucial to the AI boom, overcoming US efforts to limit Beijing’s access to the systems.

China’s chip giant Shanghai Yuliangsheng has started production of deep ultraviolet lithography machines, according to The Information, a tech publication.

These machines, which can reach the size of a double-decker bus, use high-powered lasers to imprint designs on to silicon wafers, which are used to make chips.

Until recently, only Western companies and allies of the US had the capability to produce these machines.

The most advanced versions of the technology have largely been the preserve of companies such as Dutch giant ASML and Japan’s Nikon.

These machines have been cut off from China by US export controls, preventing their production of advanced chips as Washington seeks to slow the development of AI in the country.

Semiconductor stocks plunged on the report. Trading was briefly halted on South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index after it suffered a collapse of nearly 11pc overnight, following a bleak day on Wall Street.

Advanced semiconductors, such as those used in AI chips, rely on minuscule circuits, invisible to the naked eye. They can only be manufactured by directing tiny lasers onto microchip wafers, a process known as ultraviolet lithography.

News.title: Ramsay-Peaty ‘human first, athlete second’ as he settles for second bronze
News.content:
So a pair of bronze medals for the man who once only dealt in gold. Not that Adam Ramsay-Peaty thinks that is necessarily such a bad trade when he also computes the wider price of sporting domination.

“I’ve been that person who wins all the time, and it costs you pretty much everything, and I won’t say it’s worth it,” Ramsay-Peaty said after his return to international competition continued in his now favoured 50m breaststroke with a second podium place at these Commonwealth Games. “That period of time, where I was undefeated for eight years, it was athlete first, then human,” he added. “Now it’s human first, then athlete, which is a very fair price to pay.”

Aged 31, and with a baby girl on the way with wife Holly Ramsay, Ramsay-Peaty’s order of priorities might be understandable, but it was still another performance to raise questions over whether he can again climb to the top of a major podium.

Swimming is not kind to the over-30s – Michael Phelps was the first man in 2016 to win an Olympic gold in the pool even at the age Ramsay-Peaty is now – and we still have another two years until the Los Angeles Olympics. It would be the greatest achievement even of the Englishman’s extraordinary career to win his third individual Olympic title.

He trailed from the start here and was almost exactly a second outside his world record – set almost a decade ago – as Australia’s Sam Williamson completed a breaststroke double ahead of South Africa’s Michael Houlie in second. “As you get older, it gets harder,” said Ramsay-Peaty, before adding a crucial caveat, “but I’m enjoying it more…in my head, I’m getting fresher.”

News.title: Musk passed ‘slow death sentence’ on HIV patients by cutting US spending, says head of UNAIDS
News.content:
The world’s richest man has passed a “slow death sentence” on an untold number of people with HIV by cutting US spending on the disease, according to the head of UNAIDS.

In an interview with the Telegraph, Winnie Byanyima, executive director of the UN body, said Elon Musk’s claim that the cuts made to US aid had resulted in “zero” deaths was born of ignorance.

“I do not know where Elon Musk gets his data from, but he [is] showing ignorance of the disease”, Ms Byanyima told the Telegraph at the opening the 26th International Aids Conference in Rio de Janeiro.

“This disease is not like a bullet shot in the head and you die. This is an attack on the immune system.” Withdrawing medication is a “a slow death sentence,” she said.

Data released by UNAIDS show that reductions to international funding and cuts to HIV prevention and community services threaten a resurgence of the epidemic.

In 2025, 1.2 million more people became infected with HIV and 570 000 more people died of Aids-related illnesses as the world fell short of global targets.

Although new HIV infections and Aids-related deaths are at their lowest levels in more than 30 years, an 18 per cent cut to total international funding means previous gains are now at risk, say experts.

News.title: Europe faces energy crisis as gas stockpiles sink
News.content:
Britons face a winter of surging energy bills as Europe struggles to secure enough gas to fill its storage tanks.

A squeeze on Qatari gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has pushed European gas stockpiles into “energy crisis territory”, analysts at Wood Mackenzie warned.

The Continent’s storage tanks are barely 50pc full, a historical low for this time of year. Fresh tension between the US and Iran has cut the chances of more tankers sailing anytime soon.

Wood Mackenzie now forecasts that Europe will enter the winter with its gas storage tanks no more than 75pc full, compared with a five-year average of 90pc.

This could drive up prices, as Europe competes with Asia to buy extra gas, mostly from America on the spot market.

“Europe is approaching energy crisis territory,” Wood Mackenzie warned on Monday.

Meanwhile, Britain, which no longer stores significant amounts of gas, faces paying even more than rival buyers.

“The UK’s market model is that we’ll always pay more than anyone else, rather than relying on storage,” said David Lewis, an energy analyst at Wood Mackenzie.

“If other markets are going to struggle, it just means that the UK price will be even higher.”

Last week British Gas boss Chris O’Shea warned the country risked shortages over winter because of low levels of storage.

European gas prices fell at the fastest pace in a month on Monday after a pause in attacks between the US and Iran over the weekend, dropping to about €58 per megawatt hour.

Goldman Sachs expects the price to remain at about this level for the next three months, which is 80pc higher than the pre-war price of €32.

But the US investment bank warned the price could hit €100 next year if Middle East energy exports were slow to get back to normal.

The pressure from lost Qatari supply is being compounded by the EU’s plan to prohibit imports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) from next year.

This will leave Europe in a bidding war with Japan and China for US LNG supplies.

Britain produces half its own gas and imports the rest, mostly via pipeline from Norway. But the Norwegian gas will largely track global LNG prices.

Laura Page, of the analysis firm Kpler, said Britain’s heavy reliance on Norway left it perilously exposed to any supply interruption.

“If there was a pipeline outage in Norway, or a problem with the gas field, that could cause prices to increase,” she said.

Mr Lewis said the Norwegians were postponing as much maintenance on their gas rigs as possible, to keep the supply flowing for Europe’s depleted stockpiles.

“But the problem is the same as in the UK: these are mature fields, they require a lot of maintenance, a lot of careful management,” he said.

Goldman Sachs said Europe had “only small room for error” in its gas stockpiling, and capacity could be as low as 28pc by the winter’s end.

Mr Lewis said the Netherlands and Germany were particularly exposed. “They might struggle to actually deliver the gas during peak demand days,” he said.

The El Nino weather pattern that will prevail for the rest of this year might come to Europe’s aid, delivering a milder winter than usual.

“It’s going to be an expensive winter unless we have a mild winter, which is what everybody’s hoping for at the moment. Fingers crossed,” Mr Lewis said.

News.title: Amazon has ended support for pre-2013 Kindles. What to do if you’re affected (and what to avoid)
News.content:
It seems like a lot of devices, but Amazon told Engadget that the move will affect around three per cent of current users. In theory, if you’re using a device that’s affected, then Amazon should already have notified you via email. If in doubt, however, the company has a support page with pictures and specifications of every Kindle ever released. If you’re still unsure, entering the model number into Google should reveal the exact version you’re using. This can typically be found on the back of devices.

For Kindle Fire tablets, the process is simpler. Open the Settings menu and select “Device Options”. You’ll find the model you’re using either under “Device Model” or “About Fire Tablet”.

Why did this happen?

Nobody expects electronic devices to be supported forever, but it’s disappointing that the Kindle’s most enthusiastic early adopters got cut off. Given the basic functionality of e-book reader technology, there doesn’t appear to be a technical reason behind the decision, making it appear like an anti-consumer move to push older customers towards the purchase of newer devices where existing Kindles would become an e-waste casualty.

When asked why these devices were losing support, we received a response defending the (admittedly impressive) longevity.

“These models have been supported for at least 14 years – some as long as 18 years – but technology has come a long way in that time, and these devices will no longer be supported moving forward,” an Amazon spokesperson said. “We are notifying those still actively using them and offering promotions to help with the transition to newer devices.”

At the initial time of writing, the promotions mentioned appeared to be 20 per cent off “select new Kindle devices” alongside a £15 eBook credit. While the latter was welcome, the highlighted discount is somewhat disappointing for a number of reasons. Firstly, according to the promotion’s terms and conditions, the “select” caveat excludes the most expensive model, the Kindle Scribe. It doesn’t apply to Fire devices for those tablet owners looking to replace like-for-like, either.

More importantly, the prices aren’t all that impressive considering happy owners of older Kindles weren’t budgeting for this purchase. Amazon frequently discounts its own-brand devices like Echo smart speakers and Fire tablets, and 20 per cent isn’t that unusual. Last year’s Black Friday sale saw discounts of over 30 per cent on the basic Kindle and Kindle Colorsoft, and the price-tracking site CamelCamelCamel shows that the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition has been as low as £183 in the past – a 32 per cent discount on its current price of £269.

There was added time pressure, too. Amazon said the discount and credit offer was only valid until June 20, one month after support for the older Kindles ended.

Additionally, owners of the earliest UK Kindle will see that prices have gone up over the past decade. The £109 they paid in 2010 is some way off the £159.99 Kindle Paperwhite, even with a 20 per cent discount, let alone the £219.99 Kindle Colorsoft. That said, at £94.99, the basic Kindle 12th Generation remains a bargain for no-frills readers, with a 20 per cent discount taking it down to £75.99.

Possible upgrades

If you’re affected by this news, the silver lining is that while e-book technology moves relatively slowly, things have still advanced significantly in the past 14 years. Resolutions are higher; most are backlit for bedtime reading; there’s support for audiobooks; and storage has increased. There are also optional extras like colour screens, blue-light filters to prevent eye strain and waterproofing.

As outlined in our guide to the best Kindles, our pick for most people is the 12th Generation Kindle Paperwhite, which costs £159.99 with lockscreen ads or £169.99 without. The seven inch screen with warm lighting makes for a comfortable reading experience, and it’s waterproof for bathtime or poolside reading.

At £94.99 (or £104.99 without ads), the basic 11th Generation Kindle is a great budget pick, however. It’s slightly smaller at six inches, and like the Paperwhite, can hold around 8,000 e-books with support for audiobooks through Audible. It lacks the warm light and waterproofing, however, and its battery life is around half that of the Paperwhite — albeit still a generous six weeks of normal use.

The two remaining Kindles occupy specific niches. The Kindle Colorsoft has a colour screen, making it well suited to those who enjoy graphic novels. The Kindle Scribe, meanwhile, has a bundled stylus for note taking.

Can I still use my old Kindle?

Yes, Amazon said users would be able to “continue to read books already downloaded on these devices”. If you factory reset your older Kindle, however, or you deregister it, you won’t be able to use it anymore.

Sports.title: Liverpool legend Glenn Hysen, 66, reveals he has Parkinson’s disease as he opens up on diagnosis
Sports.content:
RED'S DIAGNOSIS Liverpool legend Glenn Hysen, 66, reveals he has Parkinson’s disease as he opens up on diagnosis

LIVERPOOL icon Glenn Hysen, 66, has revealed he has been diagnosed with Parkinson’s

The Swedish star featured 72 times in the league for the Reds between 1989 and 1992.



But now he has shared the worrying diagnosis in an interview with Swedish outlet Hant.

Thankfully, Hysen was diagnosed with a mild form of the disease, and claims that he is not expected to deteriorate provided he maintains a regimen of medication.



He said: “I take medication 3-4 times a day with tablets. It’s not dangerous, but you have to treat it.”

The former defender, who made 68 appearances for his national side, certainly appears to be taking the news well.



He was in high spirits as he broke his silence on the ordeal.

He said: “I’m not the kind of person who digs deep into things. I have no problem with it, it’s not a big deal.

“I could probably work in a bar now and shake a drink.”

He explained that his symptoms flare up most when he is nervous, such as in particularly busy areas.



He added: “There are certain situations where you get a little nervous. If there are a lot of people around, I shake a little, but otherwise it’s calm.”

Hysen’s peak came when he won the Football League First Division title with Liverpool in the 1989/90 season.

He was also a three-time domestic champion and two-time Uefa Cup (now the Europa League) winner with his hometown team IFK Goteborg.

He also enjoyed spells with PSV Eindhoven and Serie A outfit Fiorentina during his 16-year career.

Sports.title: European stadium undergoing major transformation to add ROOF and boost capacity to 18,500
Sports.content:
A STADIUM set to host European matches in just a few weeks is in the midst of major reconstruction works.

Getafe secured their spot in the Uefa Conference League play-offs by finishing seventh in LaLiga last term.



But they are now in a race against time to get the Estadio Coliseum ready for their European showdown in late August.

Getafe have been playing their home games at a reduced capacity since the revamp started in June last year.



Work has ramped up over the summer, with club bosses working towards a ground with 18,500 seats – a 2,000 increase – and a roof covering every stand.

The project still has around 18 months to go, so it will not be finished by the start of the new season.

But construction chiefs are rushing to get it to a point where it meets Uefa regulations in time for their Conference League assignment.

European football‘s governing body sets out regulations on floodlighting, media infrastructure, hospitality areas and various other facilities for a stadium to be granted permission to host Uefa sanctioned matches.

Getafe had been in touch with neighbouring Atletico Madrid about the prospect of playing European home games at the Metropolitano.

But they are now going full steam ahead to try and get their own ground ready in time.

The latest plans involve the demolition of the Tribuna Stand, which will be completely out of action for the start of the new season – as will the North Stand until the end of the year.

But the South and Lateral Stands are expected to be completed.



Getafe was only founded in 1983 and they moved into the Estadio Coliseum 15 years later.

The Azulones and Rayo Vallecano still attract thousands of fans despite being overshadowed by giant neighbours Atletico and Real Madrid.

ROBERTO MANCINI is set to make a sensational return to the Italy dugout – after Andrea Pirlo’s appointment was blocked.

Sports.title: How Arsenal transfer target Vinicius Jr effectively pays his own Real Madrid wages thanks to bizarre contract
Sports.content:
ARSENAL will have to make Vinicius Junior their highest earner if they sign him from Real Madrid this summer.

But if they can negotiate similar terms to his current Real Madrid contract, the Gunners might find that the Brazilian pays for his own wages over time.



Vinicius has become a commercial juggernaut in recent years and has positioned himself as one of the most marketable players in world football.

The winger currently has a roster of 16 different sponsors that help him pocket huge sums on top of his Los Blancos salary.



Those partnerships include deals with huge brands such as Lego, Fortnite, Pepsi, Prada, Nike and Gatorade.

According to Spanish outlet AS, Vinicius’ current terms in Madrid see the LaLiga giants take 50 PER CENT of all of his image rights.



That means Real can make a killing from the sponsorships and brand deals that Vinicius lands during his time at the Bernabeu, splitting every penny equally.

It has led to jokes in Spanish media that Vinicius pays for his current £400,000-per-week salary himself thanks to how marketable he is.

Vinicius has just one year remaining on his current terms in the Spanish capital and has reopened talks with Real about a new deal this week.

The club are keen to keep hold of their star player, but will want to avoid losing him on a free transfer next summer if they can’t negotiate new terms.

If they were to do that with Vinicius, it could make a North London switch an even more attractive prospect for the star.

Arsenal could still drive huge revenue from signing Vinicius in other ways.

Sports.title: Xabi Alonso left with easy transfer decision as Chelsea win Western Sydney Wanderers goalfest
Sports.content:
For an hour in Sydney, Liam Delap was one of just a few established Chelsea players in a youthful team for the Blues' latest pre-season commitment.

When Delap left the field with Xabi Alonso's side 3-2 down, not only had he been outshone by a handful of Chelsea's army of teenage prodigies, but his replacement, Joao Pedro, emphasised why he is Chelsea's main man up front.

No sooner had he taken to the pitch, he had created the equalising goal for Jamie Gittens with some fine work. And the Brazilian then plundered the most rapid of hat-tricks in the dying embers of the game to ensure the Blues came out on top in a topsy-turvey game which finished 6-4.

In reality, there are plenty of reasons why Delap is likely to be among a number of players offloaded by Chelsea this summer, just 12 months after he was persuaded to pick the Blues ahead of numerous other top-flight suitors.

It's a transfer that just hasn't worked out for either of the parties involved. And a parting of the ways probably benefits everyone, too.

Man Utd stance on hijacking Chelsea's Danny Welbeck transfer after secret talks READ MORE :

Chelsea line up shock Danny Welbeck swoop after Xabi Alonso green lights transfer READ MORE :

In fairness to Delap, he is far from the only Chelsea signing of the Blue Co era to have been scrutinised. In fact, while some have scoffed at the idea of adding a couple of elder statesman to the squad in the form of Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson, those moves, plus the failed pursuit of Granit Xhaka earlier in the summer, have started to convince people that the Blues have rediscovered their sanity in the transfer market after years of scattergun recruitment.

At 35, Welbeck certainly isn't coming in to lead the line for 38 games in the Premier League with all hopes of a title challenge pinned upon him. But he will be a very capable, and shrewd, deputy to Chelsea's first-choice No 9 in Pedro. And that means departures will be needed.

Where that leaves Delap, largely anonymous and goalless in an entertaining if messy goalfest here, is effectively no man's land.

Bar a driving run and wild strike towards the end of the first half, Delap's impact was minimal and, as mentioned, it was some of his younger colleagues who really seized the opportunity to make an impression on their new manager. Dastan Satpayev, who does not officially join Chelsea until next month, gave Chelsea the lead with a neat finish after being played in. And it was 17-year-old Reggie Walsh who stole the show from midfield in the first half.

View 2 Images Liam Delap started the match up front for Chelsea but failed to impress with his future up in the air (Image: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC)

With a deal for Welbeck advancing at speed, if ever there was a time for Delap to catch the eye, this was probably it. It's hard to see how he fits in with him, Pedro and Strasbourg's Emmanuel Emegha all vying for minutes this season.

Delap feels like the odd man out. Perhaps his selection here emphasised that; it wouldn't be a complete shock if he or the two other players with senior appearances he started with, Tosin Adarabioyo and Josh Acheampong were not involved in Alonso's immediate first-team plans, though the latter surely would not be offloaded permanently as he surely has a future at Stamford Bridge.

For Delap, the writing was already on the wall. And nothing he did in Sydney is likely to change that.

Sports.title: Harry Kane at 33: Premier League return stance, Ballon d'Or hopes and England future
Sports.content:
This was supposed to be the icing on the cake. Harry Kane would lift the World Cup trophy and lap up the glory over the next nine days before celebrating his 33rd birthday, feeling on top of the world.

But instead, Kane will be surrounded by his loved ones as he blows out the candles, no-doubt privately ruing what could've been. The striker enjoyed his best ever season in terms of goals in 2025-26, scoring an obscene 61 times in just 51 games for Bayern Munich.

Kane fired the German giants to a dominant league and cup double, and was agonisingly close to reaching his second Champions League final, as Bayern came out on the wrong side of an 11-goal semi-final thriller with eventual winners Paris Saint-Germain. Recharged and ready to go for the World Cup, Kane started with a bang by scoring two goals against Croatia.

Another double against DR Congo saved England from a humiliating round-of-32 exit before his familiar struggles in the latter stages began. The former Tottenham star didn't score from open play in the remaining games, as Argentina ultimately dealt the fatal blow for Thomas Tuchel's side.

‌



The debate over Kane's performances in the biggest games will therefore linger for at least another season. As will the questions over the 33-year-old's future with both Bayern and England.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Harry Kane tells England teammates where they must improve before Euro 2028 READ MORE :

Harry Kane reveals England dressing room's verdict on Thomas Tuchel amid fan frustration READ MORE :

A return to the Premier League?

When Harry Kane finally decided to leave Tottenham in August 2023, he swapped a good chance to become the Premier League's all-time leading goalscorer for near-enough guaranteed team honours. Barring a disastrous first season - albeit not for him personally - in which Bayern went trophyless, his move to Bavaria has proved a success.

However, his four-year contract expires next summer. Kane won't be going anywhere for now, having decided against activating a clause in his contract which would've allowed interested clubs like Barcelona to sign him for £64million, but talks over a new deal are yet to yield an agreement.

‌



You may remember that Kane was frequently criticised for committing his long-term future to Tottenham in 2018 and making it difficult for clubs to prise him away. So, will he take a different approach this time around and leave his options open?

Should Harry Kane sign a new contract with Bayern Munich? Have your say in the comments section.

View 4 Images (Image: Alex Grimm/Getty Images)

Speaking last October, Kane revealed that his stance on returning to the Premier League has changed since his switch to Bayern. "In terms of the Premier League, I don't know," he admitted while on international duty at St George's Park.

‌



"If you had asked me when I first left to go to Bayern, I would have said for sure I would come back. Now that I have been there a couple of years, I would probably say that (desire to return) has gone down a little bit. But I wouldn’t say I would never go back."

It's worth noting that Tottenham will have first refusal on Kane if he decides to leave Munich. Spurs' recent spending is aimed at making them a stable Champions League club again, potentially giving him the ideal platform for an emotional homecoming.

View 4 Images (Image: Daniel Kopatsch/Getty Images)

Ballon d'Or hopes are 'over'

Before any major trophies can be won next season, football's biggest individual accolade is up for grabs. The Ballon d'Or will be handed out in London on Monday, October 26 and Kane remains the bookies' favourite.

‌



Obviously Emmanuel Petit doesn't have a say on that. The ex-Arsenal midfielder last week accused Kane of 'disappearing' in the latter stages of the Champions League and World Cup.

"Harry Kane's Ballon d'Or chances are over," Petit told Mr Gamble. "If you base that only on the German league, okay, no problem at all. But in the Champions League and with the national team, when it started to be really hard to win, I think he disappeared.

"I can't point the finger at him because he tried everything he could, and he scored many goals, but he didn't have an impact in the big games, just like in the Champions League. So, I think there are a few names ahead of him."

One of those is Bayern team-mate Michael Olise, although France's failure to win the World Cup has significantly dented his chances. A winner from the Spain squad who lifted the trophy is a strong possibility, with Lamine Yamal and Rodri among those in contention.

‌



View 4 Images (Image: Julian Finney - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images)

'Too soon' to decide England future

In the aftermath of England's 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina, Kane was understandably desolate. Not only did it seem to be Kane's best chance of winning the World Cup after two previous attempts, it may prove to be his last.

He'll be 36 at the next World Cup and can't guarantee that he'll be leading the line for England in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. "It's too early to talk about that," a sombre Kane said in Atlanta a fortnight ago.

"I'm taking it year by year and the national team is my pride and joy. It's what I love to do most more than anything. Obviously four years is a long way away, I'm 33 this summer but it never ended with Leo (Messi) there, he's still performing at the highest level.

‌



"I never want to put a limit on these things. I'll address situations as they come, but for now it's just about processing a tough loss."

That process will go on for a while, potentially until Euro 2028 which England will co-host. Knowing Kane, he'll be hell bent on giving himself the best chance of walking up the Wembley steps as a winner at long last.

Sports.title: Vinicius Jr has already promised to join club as Arsenal handed transfer timeline
Sports.content:
Vinicius Jr has already promised to join club as Arsenal handed transfer timeline

Vinicius Jr has already made plans for his footballing career after Real Madrid

View 3 Images Vinicius Jr could be on the move (Image: Florencia Tan Jun/Getty Images)

Vinicius Jr knows the one club he'll play for after leaving Real Madrid - and it's not Arsenal. The Gunners' concrete interest in signing the Brazilian superstar emerged this past weekend with Mikel Arteta still on the hunt for a marquee attacking signing.

‌



A report from the Athletic states that a move for the 26-year-old has been approved by club chiefs if he doesn't extend his contract with the Spanish giants. Vinicius has a year left on his deal, with Madrid said to prefer a sale this summer rather than risk losing him for free if new terms can't be agreed upon.

‌



Should he remain at the Bernabeu, the Brazil international will enter his ninth season at the club. The winger has long spoken of his love for Madrid but it won't be enough to retire a Madridista.

‌



Vinicius admitted in 2023 of his plans to one day return to his boyhood club Flamengo before he hangs up his boots. He spent 11 years in the Brazilian club's academy before making his professional debut with them in 2017.

He left just a year later for Madrid as an 18-year-old but reuniting with the storied club is a promise he once made to his father, Vinicius Jose Paixao de Oliveira. Speaking to French newspaper L'Équipe in 2024, the winger said: "I believe I could stay here (at Real Madrid) my whole career, but the club of my life is Flamengo. I promised my father I would return one day. I have to honour that promise."

PSG attack Real Madrid in fresh Yan Diomande transfer statement after ending interest READ MORE :

Vinicius Jr snubs Real Madrid return to cast fresh doubt on future amid Arsenal interest READ MORE :

It's a promise he not only made to his father, but to long-time friend and international team-mate, Lucas Paqueta. The duo grew up together at Flamengo and the ex-West Ham star already secured his own return to the club earlier this year.

‌



The 28-year-old publicised the pair's private conversation after Vinicius alleged he was racially abused by Benfica's Gianluca Prestianni in a Champions League match. Paqueta said: "I’m here, now it’s just you missing. We have to fulfil what we promised."

View 3 Images Vinicius Jr began his professional career at Flamengo (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

The promise is said to have been one they made upon breaking into Flamengo's first team with dreams of dominating South American football together. Still only 26, Vinicius has several years of his prime still to play but has no plans to return to Flamengo in his mid 30s.

‌



In an interview earlier this summer, a smiling Vinicius stated: "I’m going to come back. Ah… I’m not coming back that old, eh!" Explaining the timeline of his future, he said: "I started playing very young.

"I’m not fed up, but I do miss Flamengo, you know? But I’m not going back now, no. Not in the next 3 or 4 years. I’m still 25. Come back in 8, 9 years? No, not then. I’ll be too old by then.

"I have to win the Libertadores with Flamengo, man!" Going by Vinicius' roadmap, a move back to Brazil would occur in his early 30s as he hopes to still be influential enough on the pitch to be successful with Flamengo.

Sports.title: Lisandro Martinez reveals why Argentina turned backs on Spain players lifting World Cup
Sports.content:
Lisandro Martinez reveals why Argentina turned backs on Spain players lifting World Cup

Argentina were criticised for their reaction to Spain's World Cup win as they turned their backs on the victors when they lifted the trophy - but Lisandro Martinez has explained their actions

View 2 Images Lisandro Martinez has defended Argentina after their actions in the World Cup final

Lisandro Martinez has hit back at claims Argentina showed a lack of class when they turned their backs to Spain's World Cup trophy lift.

‌



The South Americans failed in their bid to defend their world crown in North America at they were outclassed by the European champions, who scored their winner in extra-time through Ferran Torres.

‌



Argentina's dark arts tactics had been apparent in the lead-up to the final and they tried to rattle Spain. They had Enzo Fernandez sent off before tensions boiled over after the final whistle as the two teams clashed.

‌



The Argentines picked up their runners-up medals before going over to their section of the crowd before an image of them stood with their backs to Spain went viral - sparking accusations of a lack of class.

But Martinez has come out and defended their actions, insisting they were sharing a moment with their fans, not shunning the winners, whom they met and congratulated once the dust had settled.

Mohamed Salah transfer at risk of collapse as new club enters race for Liverpool legend READ MORE :

Man Utd stance on hijacking Chelsea's Danny Welbeck transfer after secret talks READ MORE :

The Manchester United defender said: "The image where we appear with our backs to the camera was because we stayed singing with our fans. It was a show of respect towards the Argentine fans, we couldn’t leave. After the final, we greeted all the Spanish players and coaching staff."

‌



Argentina's conduct was further put under the spotlight when Leandro Paredes clashed with Gavi and Eric Garcia on the pitch, while assistant coach Roberto Ayala was also involved in an altercation with Dani Olmo. Martinez though believes the backlash has gone over the top.

"I have mixed feelings. It makes me a little angry because they have no basis for generating that hatred," the Argentine added. "They say we're arrogant but maybe it says more about the people who say those things than about us. We have always been respectful to our opponents."

View 2 Images Argentina's players copped criticism for all facing away from Spain as they lifted the trophy (Image: AFP or licensors)

‌



Argentina's defeat bought their impressive tournament run to an end. Their won the Copa America in 2021, Lionel Messi's first international trophy, and then went on to claim the World Cup and defend their Copa America title.

They couldn't make it four on the bounce having seen off the likes of Egypt, Switzerland and England en route to the final. It is almost certainly Messi's last international tournament with the 39-year-old unable to enjoy the perfect swansong.

Sports.title: Andoni Iraola’s gruelling pre-season that has left Liverpool players lying on the floor
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola’s gruelling pre-season that has left Liverpool players lying on the floor

Milos Kerkez played the best football of his career under Andoni Iraola at Bournemouth - and he is confident he will have similar impact after being appointed Liverpool boss

View 3 Images Andoni Iraola is already putting his Liverpool charges through their paces

Liverpool players are already feeling the benefits of Andoni Iraola’s exhausting pre-season sessions.

‌



Milos Kerkez knows more about the new Kop boss than most and is adamant Liverpool are intent on righting the wrongs of last season. His performances under Iraola at Bournemouth made him a £40m Liverpool left-back barely 12 months ago, with his marauding, aggressive style.

‌



And the defender is clearly delighted to be working once more with the coach who afforded him the freedom to become known as one of the most exciting attacking full-backs in England during their time together on the south coast.

‌



On Iraola’s appointment, Kerkez says: “I was delighted. I worked for him before and he improved me a lot in the two years that I spent with him.

10 Liverpool deals that have changed the reputation of the Anfield transfer plan READ MORE :

“I was happy for myself but also for the team. Everyone knows what type of football he plays so I think he is the perfect fit for us.

“What makes him a special coach? The intensity. He’s not scared to play one-on-one all over the pitch, to press high and to be on the front foot always.

‌



“If you see footage of how we all are after training, all lying down, then you can see what he is preparing us for. You definitely needs legs and good condition for what he wants us to do, but we will be alright.

“He’s very professional. He likes to talk sometimes but not a lot. He doesn’t want to get too close to some players and wants to show that everyone is the same in the team, so he doesn’t want to get too close to anyone in particular. He keeps it professional, with a lot of hard work.

View 3 Images Kerkez is hoping for a much-improved second season at Anfield

‌



“For example, when we play some games with three or four teams he calls it ‘consequences’ and the losing team and the team that finishes second has to run. How much you have to run depends on what he decides in that moment, but there is always running for the team that loses. He’s intense and he likes details.

“He always told me that defending is really important, for him that is first of all, and because you are a full back you need to defend hard. Everything you can do in front of you is like a bonus. So I was always focused first on defending and then running forward to help the wingers.

“He showed me that when you do your job then you are free to do what you want, so I felt free with him. We had a good team. It was not me, we were playing well as a team at that time. He lets you be more free to do your stuff.

‌



“The guys are doing good. The first couple of sessions, they were getting used to it but now they are getting better. The guys like how he works. I like it, they like it. It is going to suit the team perfectly.”

View 3 Images Kerkez knows all about Iraola's methods after their time together at Bournemouth

Kerkez speaks of a ‘new generation’ that is being shaped during pre-season and he is relishing the opportunity to take on more seniority.

‌



“I don’t care about pressure,” he says. “It’s a normal thing that comes with the job. You play good. You play bad. It’s process, it’s all about growing.

“If you play bad, in three days you have another game. Everyone is going to forget how you played three days ago. There is always a new game coming and then you have to do good stuff. That’s it. I don’t like that pressure stuff.

“I grew up a bit different in Serbia. It’s just your job. Do your own damn job.”

Sports.title: 10 Liverpool deals that have changed the reputation of the Anfield transfer plan
Sports.content:
Liverpool for a long time were held up as the gold standard for transfer business, owing to great synergy between Jurgen Klopp and then sporting director Michael Edwards.

Together they helped turn the Reds from a floundering side to one that would conquer the Premier League and the Champions League. The side was very much built in Klopp's image with each brick being carefully placed to create a team that Pep Guardiola's regards as his greatest challenger.

Liverpool mixed smart scouting with a shrewd knowhow for a player's worth. They rarely overpaid and often they got players who left you thinking 'how did he only cost that much?'.

But after their Premier League success of 2020 the Reds began making signings, and sanctioning departures, that suggested their level had dropped. Edwards left, he would later return in a more senior role, but has again chosen to walk away.

‌



Once upon a time it felt like Liverpool didn't spend big on a player without him proving to be a major success. Now that is no longer the case.

Mohamed Salah transfer at risk of collapse as new club enters race for Liverpool legend READ MORE :

Liverpool given free run at Bradley Barcola as Arsenal make transfer decision READ MORE :

More have failed to deliver and, as they transitioned from Klopp to Arne Slot, there's undoubtedly been a period whereby the Dutchman wanted to adopt more of his personal principles, rather than living off the German's groundwork. He has ultimately been moved on and now its Andoni Iraola trying to get a tune out of a Liverpool squad that is full of talented individuals that perhaps lack an overall direction or plan.

We take a look at the signings and the exits over the last decade that made Liverpool's recruitment and retention the envy of the league, and also those that show they've become susceptible to a big deal that is yet to bear fruits.

The hits

Andy Robertson

For all the big names through the door at Anfield none represented greater value that the Scot, who was signed from Hull City off the back of their relegation to the Championship. Still, Klopp saw something in Robertson and bought him into the fold. He didn't necessarily hit the ground running, but within 12 months was one of the best performing, most energetic left-backs in the top flight and he would go on to provide years of service, rarely letting his level drop.

‌



View 5 Images Andy Robertson spent almost a decade at Anfield (Image: Jack Thomas, Getty Images)

Mohamed Salah

Signing the former Chelsea winger, who failed to cut it at Stamford Bridge, for £34million off the back of some impressive years in Serie A made sense, but still represented an element of risk. His high pace, counter-attacking style perfectly suited Klopp's system and a goal at Watford on debut would set him on course for a record breaking first season as he claimed the Golden Boot. The goals would keep coming and when he eventually left Anfield he did so as their third greatest goalscorer ever.

Phillipe Coutinho

Only months after Salah signed to compliment a frontline that included Coutinho and Sadio Mane the Brazilian was allowed to leave for Barcelona. It was clear he wanted the move and Klopp obliged, happily saying yes to the £142m deal. Whilst an elite player left, the funds they received allowed them to reinvest in areas that posed more of an issue and his departure would ultimately ignite the path to league and European glory.

View 5 Images Virgil van Dijk's arrival was one of the catalysts for the club's success (Image: 2026 James Gill - Danehouse)

‌



Virgil van Dijk

The Dutchman was effectively signed with the money Liverpool raised from Coutinho's departure, and they still had more than enough left over. Van Dijk had established himself as one of the best defenders in the Premier League, making it clear he wanted to leave Southampton, and within weeks of moving to Anfield it became clear he had taken Liverpool up a level. He also served as one of the great examples for remaining patience - the Reds wanted a defender in the summer, but waited until the January because they were convinced Van Dijk was their man.

Emre Can

Another example of Liverpool knowing when to let a player go. The German wanted a major pay rise as he embarked on contract talks with Liverpool, where he had been performing, but giving him parity with the likes of Salah was ultimately an extreme move. Liverpool chose to let him run down his deal and Can never hit those heights again, jumping around clubs in the years after.

The misses

Naby Keita

Maybe the only major Klopp investment that you looked at and thought it didn't work. He performed, but not to the level many expected after he proved to be such a hit at RB Leipzig. Liverpool signed him ahead of time, paying his £48m release clause in 2017 before he arrived a year later. It has to be said, few wouldn't have wanted him when he was tearing it up in Germany, but he never looked totally settled in the midfield and is maybe the only blot on Klopp's recruitment record.

View 5 Images Darwin Nunez never consistently lived up to the hype (Image: Robbie Jay Barratt - AMA/Getty Images)

‌



Darwin Nunez

Liverpool went after the Uruguayan forward, landing him from Portuguese side Benfica on a six-year-deal for an initial £64m in 2022. He had scope to become the club's record signing, with the fee rising to a potential £85m with add-ons, but despite having moments in the spotlight, he massively underwhelmed. He had scored against Liverpool in the Champions League but, ironically, it was his finishing and composure that continue to prove his greatest weakness before he was offloaded to Saudi Arabia.

Florian Wirtz

The playmaker was a British-record signing but former Red Jamie Carragher was quick to flag that Liverpool paying over £100m for a player didn't feel like the Merseysiders, instead seeing it as more of a Real Madrid blueprint. The Reds' system didn't necessarily lend itself to a playmaker and 12 months on Liverpool are still trying to find a position that suits Wirtz. His lengthy wait for a first goal in red also did little to help his difficult start.

View 5 Images Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz are the club's two most expensive signings, but more was expected of them both (Image: 2025 DeFodi Images)

Alexander Isak

So many questions still swirl around this deal. Liverpool broke the British transfer record twice in a matter of weeks. They went after Isak when he made it clear he wanted to quit Newcastle, but they'd already signed Hugo Ekitike, who had begun life impressively. So far Isak's move is nothing more than a disaster with injury restricting his game time, seeing him score just four times, but even when he's been fit he's looked a shadow of the sensation we saw at St James' Park.

‌



Ibrahima Konate

After highlighting their ability to know when a player should be allowed to leave, letting Konate depart on a free could age badly. Already Iraola is talking about them being thin at the back with injuries hitting their defensive line, and Konate's quality was enough to attract Real Madrid's attention.

Sports.title: Liverpool can grant Bradley Barcola’s first demand after PSG transfer
Sports.content:
Liverpool can grant Bradley Barcola’s first demand after PSG transfer

Paris Saint-Germain star Bradley Barcola would be granted his first Liverpool wish in the event he does swap the Parc des Princes for Anfield this summer

View 2 Images Bradley Barcola's transfer to Liverpool from PSG would come complete with a gift on arrival (Image: FRANCK FIFE, AFP via Getty Images)

Liverpool can offer Bradley Barcola his favoured No. 29 jersey straight away if he agrees to leave PSG for Anfield this summer. The 23-year-old has been touted for a major move to link up with Andoni Iraola's side as a replacement for Mohamed Salah.

‌



Speculation surrounding Barcola's future has kicked into overdrive since his commitments at the World Cup wrapped up. The France forward has reportedly rejected the opportunity to open fresh talks with PSG regarding a contract extension, fuelling rumours he's ready for a move to England.

‌



French reports have suggested Barcola also turned down an approach from Chelsea earlier in the summer transfer window. However, he wouldn't come cheaply following indications PSG will demand around £140million for their player, despite him having fewer than two years remaining on his existing deal.

‌



The No. 29 has remained unoccupied for Liverpool for several years and is available should Barcola decide to make the switch. The emerging talent has worn the number throughout his time at PSG since arriving from Lyon in 2023.

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Revealing his reasoning behind selecting the No. 29, Barcola previously told trading card firm Club Legacyz: "It's actually a funny story. When I was younger, I used to play FIFA.

‌



Liverpool given free run at Bradley Barcola as Arsenal make transfer decision READ MORE :

Liverpool news: Bradley Barcola gives transfer green light as target agrees huge move READ MORE :

"In the story mode with Alex Hunter, this number became symbolic for me. I thought to myself, 'The day I go pro, it'll be number 29.' And here I am, I adopted it, and now I'll never let it go."

The last player to wear the No. 29 shirt for Liverpool was former loanee Arthur Melo during the 2022/23 campaign. And it was the very same summer that Barcola began sporting the number himself in Paris.

There will, naturally, be other clubs equally capable of offering such an unusual figure from their own stockpile. Nevertheless, it's a welcome boost for the Reds that one of their primary targets can be instantly accommodated regarding his preferred shirt choice.

‌

Sports.title: Why has Hamilton received so many penalties and what have they cost him?
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has received four penalties from the stewards in the last three Formula 1 race weekends - an unusually high number for any driver over such a short period.

After his latest penalty in Sunday's Hungarian Grand Prix for speeding in the pit lane, Hamilton stated on the radio that the stewards are "handing out penalties like crazy".

The result was that Hamilton lost further crucial points in the title race, and he now trails Kimi Antonelli by 50 points in the Drivers' Championship, so have the penalties been justified?

Image: The F1 Drivers' Championship with 11 rounds remaining

British Grand Prix - false start

Finishing Position: Third

Points lost: Likely none

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player New angles of Lewis Hamilton's false start at British GP

Hamilton was handed a five-second time penalty for jumping the start at the British Grand Prix when he was deemed to be creeping forward before the lights went out.

He went on to finish third, perhaps fortunately after knocking down his pit mechanic at a late pit stop, so the penalty likely did not impact his result. Hamilton considered the penalty harsh.

"We talked in the drivers' briefing the fact that they're inconsistent with this stuff. Drivers in the past have moved and not been penalised," he said.

"We discussed that, as long as you're not moving when the last lights are on, you shouldn't be penalised. I wasn't out of my box. And they agreed. So they're looking into that for the future."

Belgian Grand Prix - causing a collision

Finishing Position: Fourth

Points lost: Up to six

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes driver George Russell spins after contact with Lewis Hamilton and his race ends on the opening lap, but was the Ferrari driver's penalty fair?

Hamilton was given a five-second time penalty for being "wholly at fault" for colliding with George Russell on the opening lap of the British Grand Prix at Turn 5.

On the inside line, Hamilton understeered into Russell and was "unable to maintain sufficient separation" which led to the contact and Russell spinning into the gravel and out of the race.

But, Russell himself said the contact was a "racing incident" even though he came off worse.

Hamilton said: "Even the driver I collided with said that it was just a racing incident. I think that one was not needed. But that cost me a lot of points."

Hamilton benefited from pitting and serving his penalty under a Virtual Safety Car, but without the penalty he would almost certainly have been on the podium rather than finishing fourth.

He may even have had a fighting chance of victory given his team-mate Charles Leclerc was only overtaken by race-winner Antonelli with 10 laps to go. A battle with Leclerc was definitely on the cards for second.

Hungarian Grand Prix Qualifying - impeding

Starting Position: Fifth

Impact: Potential to lead race and fight for win

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton's was given a grid penalty for blocking Oscar Piastri in qualifying in Hungary

Hamilton was hit with a three-grid place penalty for impeding Oscar Piastri during the final part of Qualifying at the Hungarian Grand Prix.

After completing his final Q3 run, where he did not improve, Hamilton was not told Piastri was starting his flying lap, so effectively blocked the McLaren driver through Turn 1.

"That was really just unfortunate. I take responsibility for ultimately being on track. I should have looked in my mirrors," said Hamilton.

"But I thought everyone would have been at the end of the first lap. The information I got was right at the end. A communication error."

Hamilton was not happy that Ferrari sent himself and Leclerc out first for the last Q3 runs, which partly led to the impeding incident with Piastri.

He had qualified second and, with brand-new soft tyres, would have had a golden chance to take the lead on the first lap and potentially win the race. Instead, he started fifth and was penalised again in the Grand Prix.

Hungarian Grand Prix - speeding in the pit lane

Finishing Position: Fourth

Points lost: Up to three

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Anthony Davidson analyses Lewis Hamilton's speeding in the pit lane that handed him a five-second time penalty

The final race before the summer break was not well executed by Ferrari and Hamilton, who endured a difficult time after being overtaken by Max Verstappen after the first round of pit stops.

But Hamilton was still potentially on course for second until a Virtual Safety Car with 13 laps to go led Ferrari to pit for new fresh tyres.

In the pit lane, Hamilton exceeded the 80kph speed limit by 0.1kph as he was eager to beat Antonelli on the merge between pit exit and track.

It was a driver mistake but Hamilton thought, with hindsight, he should not have pitted and would have been third without the stop.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Max Verstappen shocks Lewis Hamilton with a stunning overtake at the Hungarian Grand Prix

"The call came literally just before the pit lane entry and I didn't have time to debate and you've got to trust the decision that has been taken," he told Sky Sports F1.

"In hindsight, my tyres were totally fine. I was probably going to lose out to Max but I think I could have kept third at least. Then just opened up the door to obviously the penalty that I got in the end."

Hamilton: I can't give stewards any reason to penalise me

Apart from the Belgium collision with Russell, all of Hamilton's penalties are hard, or impossible, to argue against. He has probably only lost six points from the in-race penalties but the impeding in Qualifying at the Hungaroring was the most detrimental.

Ferrari had great pace in Budapest and track position is king, so a good start on softs from the front row of the grid likely would have seen Hamilton in the lead.

His raw speed has been very strong recently, too, so victory was possible on Sunday and he would have been less than 40 points behind Antonelli.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton responds to his speeding penalty from Budapest

Ferrari and Hamilton must cut out these unforced errors if they want that record-breaking eighth world drivers' title.

"I'll work hard to try and come back. There's still a lot of positives to take. I'm going to try and make sure I don't give them any reason to penalise me," said Hamilton.

Sports.title: Joao Pedro nets hat-trick as Chelsea score SIX in Alonso's first game
Sports.content:
Joao Pedro scored a nine-minute hat-trick as Xabi Alonso began his Chelsea reign with a ridiculous 6-4 victory over Western Sydney Wanderers in pre-season.

Chelsea led through 17-year-old Dastan Satpaev in only the sixth minute, yet managed to fall behind three times to the A-League side before substitute Joao Pedro showed his class with a late treble in Sydney.

Alonso named a youthful side in a 4-2-3-1 formation with Tosin and Liam Delap the only significant senior experience in the starting XI before introducing the likes of Cole Palmer, Joao Pedro, Estevao and Levi Colwill midway through the second half.

How Chelsea lined up: First half: Sharman-Lowe; Acheampong, Subuloye, Tosin, Emenalo; Watson, Essugo; Kavuma-McQueen, Walsh, Satpaev; Delap.

From the 64th minute: Sanchez; Palestra, Colwill, Fofana, Anselmino; Watson, Nicoll-Jazuli; Estevao, Palmer, Gittens; Joao Pedro.

Chelsea's first two goals, the second coming from Dario Essugo, were brilliant moves from back to front on a bumpy pitch used primarily for rugby league matches, and were a sign of the style Alonso will hope to implement at Stamford Bridge.

But their defending was poor and after being level at the break, Alonso's side were trailing in the 64th minute by the time he brought on his stars, deploying Palmer in the No 10 role with Estevao on the right and Jamie Gittens on the other side.

Gittens levelled two minutes after his introduction for 3-3, yet Estevao's slack pass left youngster Reggie Watson short deep inside their own half, and Western Sydney substitute Awan Lual punished the error to restore their lead with little over 10 minutes remaining.

But then the Joao Pedro show started. He finished expertly from inside the box to bring Chelsea level again, slotted home to give them the lead after being played in by Palmer and then tapped in his third from a couple of yards at a corner to seal the win.

Sports.title: The science behind Luke Littler's trophy-laden success
Sports.content:
Want to know the secret behind the success of darting phenom Luke Littler?

Littler has spearheaded darts' surge towards the mainstream since he broke on the scene with his debut run to the 2024 World Championship final as a 16-year-old.

Darts manufacturer Target Darts has supported the global superstar since the age of 12. In February 2024, the teenager signed a multi-year mega-deal reported to be worth up to £20 million - the most lucrative the sport has ever seen.

The science behind Littler's darts

Luke Littler uses 23g Target Luke Littler Gen 1 (G1) 90% tungsten darts featuring a straight barrel design.



Barrel and Grip Specifications



Material: 90% tungsten alloy with a black PVD coating.



Weight: 23 grams.Dimensions: 52 mm length and 6.5 mm width.



Grip Design: Dual pixel grip and deep ring cuts at the front/centre, with finer radial grooves at the rear.



Shafts and Flights Setup



Points: Extended custom points (around 40mm to 45mm Swiss/nano points) for tighter grouping.



Shafts & Flights: Target K-Flex integrated flight and intermediate shaft system, typically using No.6 shape flights.



Littler possesses a generational talent when it comes to playing darts and Sky Sports pundit Wayne Mardle has said "he's probably the most natural naturally gifted player I've ever seen in my life".

Since the moment the Warrington-born star first held a dart, he's become a record-breaker and history-maker.

James Tattersall, CEO of Target Darts, says both the company and Littler are "aligned" in where they want to see the future of darts go.

Speaking at an event in which Target have set out a vision to inspire 100 million people to play darts by the end of the decade, he explained the process of how Littler sat down with chairman Garry Plummer, the design team, and engineers to build darts to perfect his game.

"I think some of the inspiration was drawn from Adrian Lewis' darts and the pixel grip, which is a unique grip that Target has and that worked its way into building up Luke's original G1," said Tattersall. "That was the barrel, but over the years Luke's tweaked it and challenged us to improve it. The point length has changed, the shaft and flight have changed to a K-Flex system before his first World Championships."

F-Flex is a one-piece flight and shaft innovation that screws into the back of the barrel.

Tattersall explained: "What it helps you do is when you're throwing darts together in such tight groupings like Luke does, the thing you want to avoid is that dart coming in and deflecting off the dart that's already in the board and the K-Flex helps reduce those deflections substantially.

"And longer points - it's like the balance of the dart and how it flies and how it lands through the air. I think another part of it is it keeps the barrel section of the dart further away from the treble and that creates more space in the board."

Talent vs Equipment?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the World Matchplay final between Luke Littler and Gerwyn Price

"His talent is all down to him," says Tattersall. "I think when you're talking about the equipment, we're talking about making Luke comfortable with all of that talent and giving him the right equipment that he's confident with to use and just to get those last few percentages, but Luke's an extraordinary player regardless."

With two world titles in three visits to Alexandra Palace, and 14 major titles to his name, Littler is well on his way to joining Phil Taylor as a legend of the sport.

The problem for his rivals is that he is still getting better after the Warrington star crushed Gerwyn Price 18-9 to retain his Betfred World Matchplay title in Blackpool on Sunday.

Littler was in imperious form as he set a new record for the final with an average of 111.53, lifting his average for the tournament as a whole to 111.04 to break Phil Taylor's previous high mark of 106.31.

The win keeps Littler on course for a clean sweep of trophies in 2026 having already won the World Championship, UK Open, Premier League and the Masters.

The supporting cast behind Littler

Image: Littler is benefitting from a huge supporting cast

Littler's management have invested in sports psychologists, nutritionists, performance coaches, and biomechanics in order to get the most out of their talent, and the teenager has benefitted in every area to help support his game.

"Mentality is absolutely key. We want to protect the players. The stage is lonely up there, and darts is a gruelling sport," Tattersall said.

"It's a bit like a penalty shootout, but every single time you're throwing a dart. It's such a closed skill, and it's so repetitive. Your mindset's got to be really, really clear, and you get those big momentum swings, you think you're about to checkout the double, you miss by a millimetre, your opponent throws in a big 170 checkout, and that's a punch in the stomach. It's how do you recover from that for the next leg? That's sports psychology, and it's crucial in all sports. I don't know why it's a surprise that it should not be in darts."

'We want to learn about action - not create robots'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Littler smashed in six brilliant 100+ checkouts as he reclaimed the World Matchplay title in Blackpool

With biomechanics, the cameras observe how a player throws darts, with sports science data helping ways of working on the technique in order to improve.

Target have ideas but Tattersall insists implementing them will not turn the Luke Littlers of this world into robots.

"That's the last thing we want to do," he said. "What we want to do is discover and learn about the sport, and learn about that action, because why is it that there are different throwing techniques?

"If you look at something like golf, where you know suddenly you come along with the Vardon grip [or overlapping grip], and that becomes almost the only way to hold a golf club.

"I think the high jump has got that really famous example of how the sport, science, innovated, [Fosbury flop], you ended up with that kind of one technique point.

"I think there will always be different ways of throwing a dart, and there will be different ways of improving those different styles, and maybe that particular style is because you're tall, and maybe that particular style is because you've got longer arms, we don't know yet, but that's what we're going to find out, and then use that data accordingly."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Littler discusses the levels he's reaching at the moment and how it compares to the legendary Phil Taylor

Zoe Burton, Chief Transformation Officer at Target Darts, says Littler is already inspiring the next generation with his natural talent, although the company are slowly moving towards a performance technology system, which is currently being tested on a number of players.

"If you look at a young person and you think of their journey as they get into a sport, you need an inspiring player - that person who they look up to - and can almost aspire to be. Luke Littler provides that," said Buton.

"You need a natural talent, but that gets you so far. Then it's determination and I think psychology as well.

"What makes a star player become a great and world-class player is actually their ability to focus under pressure and make those doubles It's never going to be robotic."

Who will win this year's BoyleSports World Grand Prix? World No 1 Luke Littler will be defending his title and you can watch all the action on Sky Sports. Stream darts and more top sport with NOW.

Sports.title: 'Never had a season like this' - Russell 'p****d off' at latest Mercedes issue
Sports.content:
George Russell says he's "never" experienced a season with so much misfortune after an engine issue caused his disastrous start to the Hungarian Grand Prix.

Russell started Sunday's race in sixth, one place ahead of Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli, but his car went into anti-stall so he slowly crept off the line and dropped to the back on the long run down to Turn 1.

He quickly moved through the field to finish seventh but lost further ground in the title race to championship leader Antonelli, who is 50 points ahead of Lewis Hamilton and 59 points in front of Russell.

"Obviously the problems are happening, but the whole team feels it as well. They're as p****d off as I am with how it's unfolded," said Russell.

"We need to look at ourselves and ensure it's nothing we're doing wrong that is contributing to these errors. Oscar [Piastri] had his [gearbox] thing as well. It's not like we're the only one, but it does feel like it is happening substantially more to me than others.

"Hopefully it swings around. I don't wish any bad luck on anyone. But I've never had a season like this in my whole career, let alone my F1 career."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch Oscar Piastri take the lead from Lando Norris as George Russell has a race start to forget at Hungaroring in Budapest

Russell explained that he was barely on the throttle pedal yet the engine was revving highly before the lights went out, which led to the "terrible start."

He told Sky Sports F1: "I was on the throttle waiting then all of a sudden the engine was going all over the place, it was revving really high and really low.

"Add it to the list of things that have happened in the first half of this year and pray things calm down in the second half."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Hungarian Grand Prix

Russell 'past the point of disappointment'

Both Mercedes drivers have suffered unreliability problems this season but Russell has been on the wrong end of things more recently.

He suffered a battery failure when fighting Antonelli for the lead at the Canadian Grand Prix, was one of five drivers to incorrectly be given a penalty for speeding in Monaco and claims to have been down on straight line speed compared to Antonelli, which culminated in a race-ending collision at the Belgian Grand Prix earlier this month.

Although he admits there are "things in my control I need to do better", Russell says "there are a lot of things out of your control".

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch all of George Russell’s unlucky moments so far this 2026 Formula 1 season

"I'm sort of past the point of disappointment now, because if I continue to be disappointed with everything that goes on, I'll just be disappointed every day of the week. So I've got to stay positive," he said.

"The pace was very strong. The team said I was as strong as anybody out there, which I haven't been there for probably three races, so I will take positives there.

"But yeah, it's just unbelievable the list of things that's happened this season."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell and Kimi Antonelli react to their respective seventh and third place finishes at the Hungarian Grand Prix

Russell was also forced to change his power unit ahead of Sunday's race after an engine crack in qualifying, meaning he may need to take a grid penalty later this year.

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said: "In terms of engine penalties, I still very much hope we don't need to take it. We need to decide when that is, when we need to take one and which tracks."
