World.title: Ensenada’s Isaac del Toro makes history at Tour de France
World.content:
Isaac del Toro has delivered Mexico’s best result ever in the Tour de France, taking third place overall and crossing the finish line Sunday in the white jersey — indicative of the race’s best young rider.

Competing in his first Tour de France, the 22-year-old from Ensenada, Baja California, stood on the podium in Paris alongside Slovenian Tadej Pogačar, who rode to a record‑equaling fifth Tour title, and Belgian Remco Evenepoel.

Isaac del Toro, winner of the white jersey at the Tour de France 👏👏😭🇲🇽🤍#TDF2026ᴿᴾ 💛 pic.twitter.com/w6DZFk3tvi — Fan Club Isaac del Toro 🐂🇲🇽 (@ToritoFanClub) July 26, 2026

Del Toro finished the three-week race 9 minutes, 42 seconds behind Pogačar, but comfortably ahead of his closest rival for the youth classification after a grueling final week in the Alps.

Evenepoel was 6:26 behind in second place following the last of 21 stages.

Early in the race, on a 168.5-kilometer stage held entirely in Spain, del Toro made history as only the second Mexican rider ever to win a stage of the Tour de France — and the first since Monterrey native Raúl Alcalá in 1989 and 1990.

On Sunday, ESPN compared Del Toro’s breakout in road cycling to Mexican pitcher Fernando Valenzuela, who won two top National League awards — the Cy Young Award, as the league’s best pitcher, and Rookie of the Year — in 1981, his first full season in the major leagues.

Del Toro battled illness in the final days but leaned on team support and Pogačar’s help on key climbs, including the summit finish to Alpe d’Huez. The two ride for the eight‑man UAE Team Emirates‑XRG squad.

“It’s not easy to finish on the podium being sick, so I’m really delighted and very grateful to the team for having done this for me,” he told Eurosport.

His performances — including the Barcelona stage win in which Pogačar eased up to let his young teammate take the victory — have turned him into a national figure. According to ESPN, murals have gone up in his honor, hills have been renamed in his native Ensenada, and cycling shops in Mexico are reporting rising demand for bikes and gear.

President Claudia Sheinbaum hailed Del Toro’s achievement on social media.

“Many congratulations to young Isaac del Toro,” she wrote Sunday on X. “Mexico is very proud of your effort, dedication and this great moment that inspires an entire country. Congratulations, Isaac! May your success continue.”

Del Toro’s Tour de France finish cemented his No. 3 status in the current Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI) world rankings, behind only Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard of Denmark.

💛 The Final Top 10 of the #TDF2026. Only two riders have managed to hold onto a place in the Top 10 between 2025 and 2026: 🇸🇮 Tadej Pogacar and 🇫🇷 Jordan Jegat! 💛 Le Top 10 Final du #TDF2026. Seuls deux coureurs ont su garder une place dans le Top 10 depuis 2025 : 🇸🇮 Tadej… pic.twitter.com/eisjQXutup — Tour de France™ (@LeTour) July 27, 2026

His breakout 2025 season produced 16 victories across stage races and one‑day events, including several stage-race titles and second place overall at the prestigious Giro d’Italia.

Vingegaard, a two-time Tour de France champion, crashed out of this year’s race, suffering a broken collarbone during Stage 15 when he was in second place.

His departure opened the door for Pogačar, 27, whose fifth title tied him with Belgian Eddy Merckx, Spaniard Miguel Indurain and Frenchmen Jacques Anquetil and Bernard Hinault for the most Tour de France titles. American Lance Armstrong was stripped of his seven titles following doping investigations by cycling authorities.

With reports from ESPN, El Universal, Cycling News and the Associated Press

World.title: Hurricane Genevieve gathers strength offshore, casting stormclouds over most of Mexico
World.content:
Hurricane Genevieve briefly reached Category 5 in the early hours of Monday, becoming the first cyclone of this magnitude recorded in the eastern Pacific since Hurricane Kristy in 2024, the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC) reported.

As of 9 a.m. CST on Monday, the NHC said Genevieve was located approximately 855 kilometers south-southwest of the southern tip of Baja California Sur, with maximum sustained winds of 250 kilometers per hour and wind gusts up to 305 kilometers per hour.

The system was moving northwest at 20 kilometers per hour on a track that kept it offshore and parallel to the Mexican coast, and is expected to maintain a west-northwest to northwest track over the next two days, gradually slowing its speed.

Despite the hurricane’s strength, forecasters have ruled out any direct impact on Mexican territory, with no coastal watches or warnings in effect.

However, the generated swells are already affecting Mexico’s southwest coast and are expected to reach southern Baja California, with the risk of potentially dangerous rip currents.

Rainfall forecast for most states

According to the National Meteorological Service (SMN), cloud bands from Genevieve in the Pacific Ocean will increase the likelihood of heavy to very heavy rains in western Mexico, coinciding with the Mexican monsoon in the northwest and Tropical Wave Number 21 in the south, which will intensify the storms.

The SMN said very heavy rains are expected on Monday in at least 17 states, with particular intensity in Sonora, Oaxaca and Chiapas.

Here’s the rain forecast for Monday afternoon:

Very heavy rain with isolated intense downpours (75 to 150 millimeters): parts of Veracruz, Oaxaca, Chiapas and Tabasco.

Heavy rain with isolated and very heavy downpours (50 to 75 millimeters): parts of Sonora, Chihuahua, Durango, Sinaloa, Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, Guerrero and Puebla.

Showers with isolated heavy downpours (25 to 50 millimeters): parts of Hidalgo, México state, Mexico City, Tlaxcala, Morelos, Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo.

Periods of showers (5 to 25 millimeters): parts of Baja California, Baja California Sur, Tamaulipas, Zacatecas, San Luis Potosí, Guanajuato and Querétaro.

Isolated rain (0.1 to 5 millimeters): parts of Coahuila, Nuevo León and Aguascalientes.

With reports from Radio Fórmula and the Associated Press

World.title: MND Local: Experiencing a taste of Oaxaca at its annual mezcal festivals
World.content:
July sees hundreds of thousands of visitors arriving in Oaxaca to celebrate (and photograph) the traditions of Guelaguetza. Many are on the hunt for the best mezcal, and there are many events to provide just that, ranging from tasting seminars to street parties.

The principal event in Oaxaca City is the Feria del Mezcal, hosted at the Centro Cultural y de Convenciones de Oaxaca (CCO) in Santa Lucía del Camino. This is a multi-day extravaganza concluding July 28. Although many treat the event like the world’s largest open bar, it is much more than that. It is an agro-industrial, cultural exhibition where you can find rare mezcals and meet the producers who make them.

Oaxaca’s mezcal sipping and sampling festivals

Glynn Pegler runs two bars in Oaxaca City and says he has seen a “noticeable increase in the professionalism of the Feria this year. There is a full program of entertainment and seminars, and stricter controls on the quality of the products and their authenticity. From the quality of the displays and decorations in each of the mezcal stands this year, it is clear that everyone in the Feria has upped their game.”

Santiago Matatlán is a Oaxacan town known as “the World Capital of Mezcal.” The town recently hosted its own “Grand Mezcal Festival,” held from July 23-26, 2026. The dates coincided with the state celebration of Guelaguetza, as well as the town’s saint’s day (July 25) honoring Santiago Apóstol.

This year, the fair took place just a few blocks from the town square. Stalls showcased local mezcal brands, as well as traditional crafts and food. Over the course of the event, experts including Mabi Cuish, Carmen Vásquez and Cynthia Villalobos gave lectures. Music and dancing were featured in the form of a calenda, a cabalgata (horseback procession) and a jaripeo (rodeo).

An education in mezcal

The celebration integrates the mezcal tradition with other elements of Oaxaca’s cultural identity, strengthening the tourist offerings of Santiago Matatlán and its connection with Guelaguetza activities.

On Saturday, organizers presented awards, cheered on by the festival crowd. These included diplomas for students who completed a course in mezcal production through the “University of Mezcal.” The main event was the Largest Agave Heart Contest, sponsored by ProMez. The contest recognizes the quality and effort of the producers, highlighting two fundamental aspects of the agave: its sugar content, measured in degrees Brix, and the weight of the hearts.

Although the Grand Mezcal Festival in Matatlán has finished, you can still visit the community and the mezcal producers who work there. You can do this by reaching out to mezcalerías such as Quiote or by contacting local guides.

Anna Bruce is an award-winning British photojournalist based in Oaxaca, Mexico. Just some of the media outlets she has worked with include Vice, The Financial Times, Time Out, Huffington Post, The Times of London, the BBC and Sony TV. Find out more about her work at her website or visit her on social media on Instagram or on Facebook.

World.title: 2 separate freight derailments prompt emergency responses
World.content:
In two separate incidents on Saturday night, a tank car on a freight train derailed, prompting the mobilization of emergency services while specialized personnel carried out containment efforts.

Authorities declared a Code Red in the northern state of Tamaulipas, Mexico, after a Pemex-owned tank car carrying 70,000 liters of gasoline tipped over when a freight train derailed.

The incident, which occurred in the Kansas City Southern rail yard in Ciudad Madero, triggered hazardous materials response protocols.

Municipal, state and federal authorities cordoned off the perimeter and established a command post. Specialized personnel quickly evaluated the scene to consider the possibility of leaks, fire hazards and explosion risks.

The situation was fraught with danger as the Ferrocarrilera Talleres neighborhood — the site of the accident — is one of the most sensitive railway and industrial corridors in southern Tamaulipas. Its proximity to logistics infrastructure linked to Petróleos Mexicanos — including the Madero Refinery — prompted authorities to consider an evacuation, though it was deemed not necessary.

Local officials urged the public to avoid the area while the authorities continued trying to secure the tanker truck, citing the risk posed by any maneuver involving a vehicle loaded with fuel. Authorities — along with Pemex personnel — were preparing to transfer the fuel to a different tank car on Monday.

As of Sunday night, authorities had not reported any injuries or fuel spills.

Evacuarán a más de 200 personas en Ciudad Madero por retiro de carrotanque con gasolina descarriladohttps://t.co/HiyEL5wEg4 pic.twitter.com/HJXrx1dTuh — Milenio Tamaulipas (@MilenioTam) July 27, 2026

In the second incident, a freight train derailed in the municipality of Naco, Sonora, approximately 20 miles south of the U.S. border.

The derailment occurred just outside the town of Ejido Cuauhtémoc on the railway tracks used by Ferromex, a private rail transport company that operates the largest freight railway network in Mexico.

According to official information from the Sonora civil protection agency, one of the tank cars overturned during the derailment, causing the spillage of a chemical substance.

Although neither the type of chemical involved nor the volume of the spilled material was specified, specialists were inspecting the site to define remediation measures and rule out additional risks.

Emergency personnel were carrying out assessment, monitoring and control work to determine the extent of the spill and reduce any risk to the environment and ensure public safety.

The area remains under precautionary protection while technical operations continue to determine the cause of the accident, to recover the spilled chemical and to ensure safe conditions before resuming rail operations.

The incident occurred less than two weeks before the 12th anniversary of one of the biggest environmental disasters in Mexico’s history. On Aug. 7, 2014, a chemical spill despoiled the Sonora River, affecting more than 22,000 inhabitants across eight municipalities.

With reports from La Jornada, Hoy Tamaulipas, Nación 321 and El Sol de Tampico

World.title: Modern tech and an old find combine to shed new light on the Maya
World.content:
The digital reconstruction of a charcoal mural discovered more than two decades ago in the ancient Maya city of Calakmul, Campeche, has revealed the earliest known evidence of calendrical writing in Calakmul, the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) reported.

Until this discovery, there was no evidence of early written communication in Calakmul, as most of its known inscriptions date from the Classic period (250-900 CE).

“Now, we can include Calakmul as one of the places where these types of manifestations exist,” head of the research project Daniel Salazar Lama said in a press conference.

Measuring 1.90 meters wide by 1.70 meters high, the painting depicts the mythical Maya hero Juun Ajaw hunting a creature in the water. Next to him is a symbol corresponding to a day marker within the 260-day ritual calendar cycle known as Tzolk’in.

The mural could represent an episode in the life cycle of the maize god, likely a propitiatory or renewal ritual, Salazar explained, adding that the calendrical date appears to have been drawn after the main scene, commemorating the hunting and sacrificial episode featuring Juun Ajaw.

Salazar said that this discovery places Calakmul at the “center of the cultural explosion of the Maya Lowlands during the Late Preclassic period [400 BCE-250 CE],” alongside cities such as San Bartolo, El Mirador and Tikal — all in Guatemala — recognized for their monumental architecture and early writing.

New technologies shed light

The mural was found inside an arched vault at Calakmul, as part of the Calakmul Archaeological Project led by archaeologist Ramón Carrasco Vargas, after which it was transferred to the National Coordination for the Conservation of Cultural Heritage in 2005 for study and conservation.

Because the painting was in poor condition upon discovery, scientists had been unable to appreciate the scene with the naked eye. But modern techniques, including photogrammetry and digital drawing, made it possible for researchers to finally reconstruct the artwork.

The new technology also provided new evidence about the mural’s age.

The building housing the mural was originally thought to have been built between 400 and 390 BCE, but scientists now believe it dates from between 400 to 200 BCE. The drawing style itself also supports this theory. However, further samples are needed to pinpoint the date.

Archaeologists also determined that the chamber containing the mural was deliberately designed to evoke the interior of a cave, a space of profound cosmological significance for the Maya.

World.title: Northeast Brazil Wins New Beef Plants and Shoe Factories
World.content:
Industrial Expansion

Key Facts —Masterboi plant. A R$120 million (US$24 million) beef slaughterhouse in Canhotinho, Pernambuco, will process 700 cattle daily and create 800 direct jobs. —NKS factory. A R$40 million (US$7.9 million) footwear plant in Cariré, Ceará, aims to produce 200,000 pairs monthly and employ 1,200 workers. —MRS Calçados. A R$7.5 million (US$1.5 million) unit in Catunda, Ceará, is already operating and targets 4,000 pairs per day with 400 jobs. —Neorubber sandals. An R$8 million (US$1.6 million) plant in Crateús, Ceará, will produce 30,000 pairs and generate over 500 jobs. —Export gateway. The Masterboi plant holds SIF federal inspection status, unlocking direct access to international meat markets for the region.

Northeast Brazil investments are surging as a new R$120 million Masterboi beef plant in Pernambuco and three footwear factories in Ceará promise over 3,000 direct jobs and deeper integration into global export chains.

Northeast Brazil Lands Billions in New Beef Plants and a Shoe Factory (Photo internet reproduction)

Masterboi brings export-grade beef processing to Pernambuco

Masterboi, a company already operating two industrial units in Brazil’s North region, is building its first Northeast slaughterhouse in Canhotinho, Pernambuco. The R$120 million (US$24 million) facility is designed to be the largest beef plant in the Northeast.

It is also the only plant in the region with Federal Inspection Service (SIF) status, a certification that opens doors to international markets. Initial capacity stands at 700 head of cattle per day, with plans to scale up to 1,400 animals and process 300 tons of meat daily.

The project is expected to create around 800 direct jobs and between 3,000 and 3,500 indirect positions. It also handles sheep, goats and pigs, broadening its production base across the semi-arid livestock belt.

Ceará cements its role as Brazil’s footwear powerhouse

Three new footwear projects in Ceará are adding muscle to a state that already accounts for a dominant share of Brazilian shoe exports. The largest is NKS Vulcanizados, investing R$40 million (US$7.9 million) in a Cariré plant with 10,000 m² of built area; the Ceará government initially projected 1,200 direct jobs, while a more recent state announcement cites 800 formal jobs over three years.

NKS plans to reach 200,000 pairs per month by its third year and employ 1,200 people directly. The investment reflects a deliberate strategy of geographic diversification by a company positioning itself as a national supplier.

In Catunda, MRS Calçados has already started operations after negotiating terms with state and local authorities. The company committed R$7.5 million (US$1.5 million) through 2026 and currently produces 750 pairs daily, with a target of 4,000 pairs and up to 400 direct jobs.

Neorubber and the sandal export engine

A third project, Neorubber Sandals Industry in Crateús, signed a cooperation agreement for an R$8 million (US$1.6 million) plant. It will produce around 30,000 pairs of footwear across three warehouses totalling 7,200 m².

The unit is expected to generate more than 500 job openings. It fits neatly into Ceará’s specialisation in rubber and vulcanised footwear, a segment that has driven export growth of 39.2% in recent years, reaching US$221.4 million in the first nine months of 2022 alone.

Major players like Vulcabras have already poured over R$320 million into modernising Ceará operations, calling the state “the best place for shoe production in Brazil.” The new entrants reinforce that conviction.

Why Northeast Brazil investments are shifting the industrial map

These projects are not random. They reflect a decades-long relocation of Brazil’s beef and footwear industries from the traditional South and Southeast clusters toward the Northeast, drawn by lower labour costs, tax incentives and improving infrastructure.

By 2010, the Northeast already produced about 45% of Brazil’s shoes and 71% of footwear exports. The new Ceará plants deepen that concentration, while the Masterboi facility brings large-scale, export-certified beef processing to a region long seen as a livestock frontier rather than a processing hub.

For investors, the pattern is clear: interior municipalities such as Canhotinho, Cariré, Catunda and Crateús are being wired into national and global supply chains. The combined committed capital across these four projects comfortably exceeds R$175 million (US$34 million).

What this means for markets, exports and expat business

The SIF certification on the Masterboi plant is the strategic prize. It allows direct beef exports from Pernambuco, bypassing the need to ship cattle south for processing and certification, which cuts logistics costs and opens new trade corridors.

Brazil is already the world’s largest beef producer, with giants JBS, Marfrig and Minerva controlling roughly half the domestic market. Masterboi’s Northeast entry adds a competitive independent player into an export-oriented landscape.

On the footwear side, Ceará’s rubber-shoe exports to the United States have been the standout growth driver. For expat entrepreneurs and sourcing professionals, the cluster effect in Ceará means denser supplier networks, trained labour pools and established logistics routes.

The local development dividend

Beyond the export numbers, these projects deliver a direct development impact on small interior towns. The 3,000-plus direct jobs and several thousand indirect positions diversify local economies that have historically depended on subsistence agriculture and government transfers.

State governments in Pernambuco and Ceará have actively courted these investments with tax packages and infrastructure support. The payoff is a more resilient economic fabric in municipalities that previously sat far from industrial value chains.

For policymakers, the lesson is that industrial decentralisation works when paired with sector-specific incentives and export certification. For investors, the signal is that the Northeast is no longer just a cost play but an increasingly capable production platform.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Masterboi building its first Northeast plant in Pernambuco?

Masterboi chose Canhotinho, Pernambuco, to tap the semi-arid region’s large cattle herd and gain SIF federal inspection status, which allows direct meat exports. The R$120 million plant fills a gap in large-scale, export-certified beef processing in the Northeast and brings slaughtering capacity closer to livestock producers, reducing transport costs.

How many jobs will the new Ceará shoe factories create?

The three new footwear projects in Ceará—NKS Vulcanizados in Cariré, MRS Calçados in Catunda, and Neorubber in Crateús—are expected to create more than 2,100 direct jobs combined. NKS alone accounts for 1,200 positions, while MRS and Neorubber add up to 400 and over 500 jobs respectively, with additional indirect employment in each municipality.

What makes Ceará a leading footwear exporter in Brazil?

Ceará has attracted major footwear manufacturers through lower labour costs, state tax incentives and a specialised workforce built over decades of industry relocation from Brazil’s South. The state now dominates rubber and vulcanised footwear exports, with shipments growing 39.2% to US$221.4 million in early 2022, driven heavily by demand from the United States market.

World.title: Cosan Narrows Q2 Loss as Deleveraging Drive Takes Hold
World.content:
Brazilian Conglomerates

Key Facts —Net loss. Cosan posted a R$946 million (US$186 million) net loss, R$719 million narrower than a year earlier. —Gross debt. Gross debt fell to R$21.5 billion (US$4.2 billion), helped by liability-management actions over twelve months. —Net debt. Net debt held steady at R$17.5 billion (US$3.4 billion) during the quarter. —Drivers. The improvement reflected non-recurring effects in the year-ago period, including tax credits at Raízen and Vale divestment impacts. —Strategy. Cosan said deleveraging remains the priority, with asset sales and capital-market actions used exclusively to cut leverage.

Brazil’s Cosan narrowed its second-quarter net loss to R$946 million as a disciplined deleveraging drive reshaped the conglomerate’s balance sheet, offering investors a clearer view of a leaner group.

Cosan Narrows Q2 Loss as Deleveraging Drive Takes Hold (Photo internet reproduction)

The Numbers Behind the Cosan Deleveraging Drive

Cosan reported a net loss of R$946 million (US$186 million) for the second quarter of 2025, a R$719 million improvement from the same period a year earlier. The company attributed the narrower loss largely to non-recurring effects that had weighed on the prior-year comparison, including tax credits at its Raízen joint venture and the financial impact of Vale’s divestment.

Those one-off items were partly offset by the Rumo Malha Sul impairment that had affected the earlier period. The net result, while still in the red, signalled that management’s focus on balance-sheet repair is beginning to show through the income statement.

Gross debt declined to R$21.5 billion (US$4.2 billion), down from higher levels a year ago, as liability-management actions taken over the preceding twelve months fed through. Net debt remained stable at R$17.5 billion (US$3.4 billion) during the quarter, a figure that analysts are watching closely as a gauge of the group’s financial resilience.

A Conglomerate Under Pressure

Cosan is one of Brazil’s most sprawling industrial groups, with interests spanning sugar and ethanol through Raízen, logistics via Rumo, lubricants and energy distribution, and a stake in mining giant Vale. That diversification has historically been a strength, but it also exposed the group to rising interest rates that pushed up debt-servicing costs across its operations.

Earlier quarterly losses had been linked directly to higher interest expenses, a challenge that prompted management to make deleveraging its stated top priority. The latest results suggest that message is more than rhetoric, with asset sales and targeted capital-market moves now visibly reducing the debt load.

The company has been explicit that proceeds from any divestments are being used exclusively to pay down leverage, not to fund new spending or acquisitions. That discipline marks a shift in tone from a group that once pursued growth across multiple fronts simultaneously.

What the Cosan Deleveraging Drive Means for Investors

For international investors and expats with exposure to Brazilian equities, Cosan’s trajectory offers a real-time case study in how a highly leveraged conglomerate navigates a high-rate environment. The narrowing loss and stable net debt suggest the deleveraging programme is gaining traction, even if a full turnaround remains some way off.

The group’s complexity means that headline net income can be swayed by non-cash items and one-off effects at subsidiaries, making the debt figures a cleaner signal of progress. The decline in gross debt to R$21.5 billion is a concrete marker that the balance sheet is being repaired.

Market analysts have noted that Cosan’s strategy follows a clear sequence: reduce leverage first, then rebuild growth. That sequencing matters because it determines when the group might return to the expansionary posture that once defined it, and whether it can do so without re-inflating its debt burden.

The Latin America Read-Through

Cosan’s experience mirrors a broader pattern across Latin America’s corporate landscape, where highly indebted groups are being forced to choose between deleveraging and growth. Rising global interest rates and persistent inflation in Brazil have made carrying large debt loads far more expensive than during the cheap-money years of the 2010s.

The group’s decision to prioritise balance-sheet health over expansion echoes moves by other major Brazilian corporates that have sold non-core assets and trimmed capital spending. For foreign investors, the signal is that management teams are responding to the rate cycle with greater caution than in previous episodes.

Cosan’s exposure to both energy and logistics also makes it a bellwether for two of Brazil’s most important sectors. Raízen’s performance reflects global sugar and ethanol dynamics, while Rumo’s results track the country’s agricultural export machine, giving the conglomerate an outsized role in how international markets read Brazil’s economic health.

What to Watch Next

The key metric for the coming quarters will be whether net debt continues to decline or merely stabilises at current levels. A further reduction would confirm that asset-sale proceeds and operational cash flow are being effectively channelled toward deleveraging, rather than being absorbed by working-capital needs or subsidiary-level spending.

Investors should also watch for any signals that Cosan is preparing to pivot from defence to offence. The company has been clear that growth comes second, but the timing of any shift will be critical for the share price, particularly if interest rates in Brazil begin to ease from their current elevated levels.

The performance of Raízen and Rumo as standalone entities will also matter, since Cosan’s consolidated results are heavily influenced by their trajectories. Any major operational surprises at either subsidiary would flow directly into the parent company’s deleveraging arithmetic.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Cosan’s net loss in Q2 2025?

Cosan reported a net loss of R$946 million (approximately US$186 million) for the second quarter of 2025. This was a R$719 million improvement from the same period a year earlier, driven mainly by non-recurring effects in the comparison quarter.

How is Cosan reducing its debt?

Cosan is using asset sales and capital-market actions exclusively to reduce leverage, which management has identified as the group’s top priority. Gross debt fell to R$21.5 billion in the quarter, helped by liability-management actions over the preceding twelve months, while net debt remained stable at R$17.5 billion.

What businesses does Cosan own?

Cosan is a diversified Brazilian conglomerate with interests in sugar and ethanol through its Raízen joint venture, logistics via rail operator Rumo, lubricants and energy distribution, and a stake in mining giant Vale. The group’s complexity means its consolidated results are influenced by performance across multiple sectors.

World.title: Brazil’s OceanPact Clears Antitrust Hurdle for CBO Merger
World.content:
Offshore Services Consolidation

Key Facts —CADE clearance. Brazil’s antitrust authority approved the OceanPact-CBO merger unconditionally, with no remedies required. —All-stock deal. The transaction involves issuing roughly 275 million new OceanPact shares to CBO shareholders. —Ownership split. CBO shareholders will hold about 57.86% of the combined company, with current OceanPact investors at 42.14%. —Petrobras involvement. The state oil giant participated as an interested third party and may still appeal the decision within 15 days. —Closing timeline. The parties expect to finalise the merger between the second and third quarters of 2026.

Brazil’s competition authority CADE has cleared the OceanPact CBO merger without conditions, paving the way for the creation of the country’s largest integrated offshore support platform and reshaping the maritime services landscape for Petrobras contractors.

OceanPact Wins CADE Approval for CBO Offshore Merger in Brazil (Photo internet reproduction)

CADE Clears the OceanPact CBO Merger Without Remedies

Brazil’s Administrative Council for Economic Defence (CADE) has approved the incorporation of CBO Holding S.A. into OceanPact Serviços Marítimos S.A. unconditionally. The decision imposes no structural or behavioural remedies on the parties, such as asset sales or conduct commitments.

The clearance removes the principal regulatory hurdle for a deal that will combine two of Brazil’s most prominent offshore support vessel operators. CADE’s Superintendence reviewed the transaction and concluded it did not require restrictions to preserve competition in the offshore maritime support market.

How the All-Stock Transaction Is Structured

The merger is a 100% stock transaction. OceanPact will issue approximately 274 to 275 million new shares to CBO’s shareholders in exchange for the entirety of CBO’s holding company.

Once completed, CBO shareholders will control roughly 57.86% of the combined entity’s capital. Current OceanPact shareholders will retain about 42.14%, reflecting the relative scale of the two businesses being brought together under a single publicly listed structure.

Petrobras Steps In as an Interested Third Party

Petrobras, the dominant client for offshore support services in Brazil, formally requested to participate in the CADE review as an interested third party. The antitrust body asked the state-controlled oil giant to supply detailed data and technical information on competition dynamics in the sector.

Petrobras now has 15 days from the publication of CADE’s decision to lodge an appeal before the agency’s Tribunal. While the transaction stands approved without restrictions, a challenge from the country’s largest offshore services buyer could still introduce delays.

What the OceanPact CBO Merger Means for Brazil’s Offshore Market

The combined company will operate one of Brazil’s largest integrated offshore support fleets, with dozens of vessels and a substantial contracted backlog. The consolidation creates a heavyweight contractor better positioned to serve Petrobras’s deepwater production ambitions and the expanding pre-salt fields.

For investors, the merger signals a maturing offshore services sector where scale increasingly determines competitiveness. The enlarged fleet and balance sheet should improve the group’s ability to bid for long-term charter contracts and weather the cyclical swings that have historically defined the Brazilian maritime support industry.

Timeline and What to Watch Next

The merger agreement listed CADE approval as a key condition precedent, with both companies targeting a closing window between the second and third quarters of 2026. The unconditional clearance keeps that schedule firmly on track.

Market watchers should monitor whether Petrobras exercises its appeal rights in the coming days. Beyond that, attention will shift to integration planning, fleet optimisation, and how the combined entity positions itself for the next Petrobras tender cycle.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did CADE decide on the OceanPact CBO merger?

CADE approved the incorporation of CBO into OceanPact unconditionally, with no structural or behavioural remedies. The clearance means the parties do not need to sell assets or accept conduct restrictions to complete the deal.

Who will control the combined company after the merger?

CBO shareholders will hold approximately 57.86% of the combined entity, while current OceanPact shareholders will own about 42.14%. The transaction is structured as a 100% stock deal with roughly 275 million new OceanPact shares issued to CBO’s owners.

Can Petrobras still challenge the merger approval?

Yes. Petrobras is registered as an interested third party in the CADE proceedings and has 15 days from the publication of the decision to appeal to CADE’s Tribunal.

The transaction is currently approved without restrictions, but an appeal could introduce procedural delays.

World.title: China Shifts from Buyer to Rival, Threatening Brazil Chicken Exports
World.content:
Trade & Commodities

Key Facts —Structural shift. China is expanding poultry exports of cuts like chicken breast, moving from a major buyer of Brazilian chicken to a direct competitor in third markets. —Product at risk. Chicken breast accounted for 22% of Brazil’s total poultry export volume over the past 12 months, making it a sensitive category for Brazilian producers. —Geographic pressure. China’s proximity to the Gulf states gives it a logistical advantage over Brazil in markets that are strategically important for Brazilian exporters. —Trade volatility. China imposed a countrywide ban on Brazilian poultry after avian flu was detected in May 2025, disrupting the traditional buyer relationship before later moving to restore imports. —Analyst warning. BTG Pactual flagged the risk that more Chinese production and exports could mean lower global prices and less room for Brazil in premium export cuts.

China is no longer just a major buyer of Brazil chicken exports; it is increasingly becoming a rival supplier in third markets, threatening to pressure Brazilian prices and market share in strategically important destinations like the Gulf states.

China Shifts from Buyer to Rival, Threatening Brazil Chicken Exports (Photo internet reproduction)

The Evolving China-Brazil Poultry Relationship

For years, China ranked among the largest destinations for Brazilian chicken, absorbing vast quantities of cuts that Chinese consumers favoured. That relationship has always carried volatility, with disease-related trade bans and reopenings punctuating the flow of goods.

The most recent disruption came in May 2025, when China imposed a countrywide ban on Brazilian poultry after avian flu was detected. Even as both countries worked to restore imports, a deeper structural change was already underway inside China’s poultry sector.

What BTG Pactual’s Analysis Reveals About Brazil Chicken Exports

BTG Pactual’s analysis points to a clear risk: China is expanding its own poultry exports, particularly of chicken breast, a cut less favoured domestically in China but critically important for Brazil’s export mix. Over the past 12 months, chicken breast accounted for 22% of Brazil’s total poultry export volume.

China still imports products such as chicken feet, which remain popular in its domestic market. But the shift toward exporting breast meat puts Chinese producers on a collision course with Brazilian exporters in third markets where both countries compete.

The Gulf States: A Key Battleground

The Gulf states, including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, have long been strategically important destinations for Brazilian poultry. When China’s imports from Brazil have fallen in the past, Brazil has often redirected shipments to these markets to absorb the excess supply.

China’s geographic proximity to the Gulf gives it a logistical advantage over Brazil, potentially allowing Chinese exporters to offer lower freight costs and faster delivery times. That edge could prove decisive in price-sensitive tenders and contracts across the region.

What This Means for Brazilian Producers and Investors

The structural risk is not that China has already replaced Brazil, but that its poultry sector is evolving from a destination for Brazilian exports into a rival supplier. More Chinese production and exports could translate into more competition, lower global prices, and less room for Brazil in premium export cuts.

For investors in Brazilian agribusiness, the message is one of margin pressure ahead. Companies heavily exposed to chicken breast exports may need to diversify product lines or deepen relationships in markets where China’s logistical advantage is less pronounced.

The Latin America Read-Through

Brazil is not alone in facing this shift. Other Latin American poultry exporters, including Argentina and Chile, could also feel the effects of increased Chinese competition in global markets.

The broader lesson for the region is that China’s role in agricultural trade is becoming more complex. It is no longer simply a hungry buyer but an increasingly capable producer, a dynamic that will reshape trade flows and pricing power across Latin America’s commodity-exporting economies.

What to Watch Next

Trade data over the next two quarters will reveal whether Chinese poultry exports are growing at a pace that materially erodes Brazil’s market share in the Gulf and beyond. Brazilian exporters will be watching Chinese production figures and export licence approvals closely.

Any further disease-related disruptions to Brazil’s own poultry output could accelerate the competitive shift, giving Chinese exporters an opening to lock in long-term supply contracts with buyers who might otherwise have sourced from Brazil.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is China shifting from a buyer to a rival in Brazil chicken exports?

China is expanding its own poultry production and increasingly exporting cuts like chicken breast that are less popular domestically. This puts Chinese exporters in direct competition with Brazil in third markets, particularly the Gulf states, where China’s geographic proximity gives it a logistical advantage.

How much of Brazil’s poultry exports are at risk?

Chicken breast accounted for 22% of Brazil’s total poultry export volume over the past 12 months, making it a sensitive product category. While China still imports cuts like chicken feet from Brazil, its expansion into breast meat exports directly targets a high-value segment of Brazil’s trade.

Which markets are most vulnerable to Chinese competition?

The Gulf states, including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, are strategically important for Brazilian poultry and geographically closer to China. Brazil has historically redirected shipments to Asian markets when Chinese imports fell, but Chinese exporters now have a freight-cost advantage in the same destinations.

World.title: Bazar de Bandas 2026 Hits Mexico City’s Revolution Monument

LIFE: CIUDAD DE MÉXICO

Key Facts —Dates. Bazar de Bandas 2026 runs Friday 13 March through Sunday 15 March. —New Venue. The event moves to the Explanada del Monumento a la Revolución in the Cuauhtémoc borough. —Hours. Doors are open daily from approximately 11:00 to 18:00 local time. —Admission. Entry is completely free of charge for all three days. —Format. The bazaar mixes live band merchandise, vinyl records, art, and independent fashion.

Bazar de Bandas 2026 has confirmed its official dates for 13 to 15 March at a striking new venue, the Monumento a la Revolución esplanade, marking a significant upgrade for one of the capital’s most popular independent music and culture markets.

Bazar de Bandas 2026 Sets March Date at Mexico City’s Monumento a la Revolución (Photo internet reproduction)

Official Dates and Schedule for Bazar de Bandas 2026

The organisers have locked in the weekend of Friday 13 March through Sunday 15 March 2026. The market will operate each day from roughly 11:00 in the morning until 18:00 in the evening.

This three-day format has become a staple for the event, giving attendees ample time to browse without the pressure of a single-day rush. Arriving early on Friday is often the best strategy for collectors seeking limited-edition vinyl and merchandise.

A Monumental Shift: The New Venue at Monumento a la Revolución

For 2026, Bazar de Bandas relocates to the Explanada del Monumento a la Revolución, situated at Plaza de la República s/n in the Colonia Tabacalera neighbourhood. This open-air esplanade sits in the Cuauhtémoc borough, one of the city’s most central and accessible districts.

The move places the bazaar directly in front of one of Mexico City’s most iconic landmarks. The vast paved plaza offers significantly more space than previous locations, suggesting organisers are preparing for larger crowds and an expanded vendor lineup.

What to Expect at the 2026 Edition

Bazar de Bandas is not a traditional music festival with live stages. It functions as a curated marketplace where independent and established bands sell official merchandise, from screen-printed T-shirts to rare vinyl pressings.

Beyond music, the event has grown into a broader cultural fair. Visitors can expect stalls from independent fashion designers, visual artists selling prints and zines, and food vendors offering local street-food staples.

The Business of Band Merchandise in Latin America

For independent musicians across Latin America, merchandise sales have become a critical revenue stream as streaming payouts remain low. Events like Bazar de Bandas provide a direct-to-fan retail channel that cuts out digital intermediaries.

For international visitors and expats, the bazaar offers a concentrated look at Mexico’s current music scene. A single purchase of a limited-run vinyl or a hand-printed poster can serve as both a cultural artefact and a direct injection of cash into the local creative economy.

Getting There and Navigating the Cuauhtémoc Borough

The Monumento a la Revolución is exceptionally well connected by public transport. The Revolución Metro station on Line 2 sits just steps from the plaza, and multiple Metrobús routes service the immediate area.

For those driving, public parking is available in the monument’s underground facility, though spaces fill quickly during large events. Ride-hailing services remain the most convenient door-to-door option for visitors carrying heavy bags of vinyl and merchandise.

Why Free Admission Matters for Mexico City’s Cultural Calendar

Keeping entry free removes the financial barrier that often excludes younger fans and casual visitors from cultural events. This model relies on vendor fees and high footfall, a formula that has proven sustainable for Bazar de Bandas across multiple editions.

For the city, hosting a free, large-scale event at a historic monument reinforces the public use of civic spaces. It also drives ancillary spending in nearby restaurants, bars, and shops in the Tabacalera and Juárez zones throughout the weekend.

Frequently Asked Questions

When exactly is Bazar de Bandas 2026 in Mexico City?

The official dates are Friday 13 March, Saturday 14 March, and Sunday 15 March 2026. The market runs daily from approximately 11:00 to 18:00 local time.

Where is the new venue for Bazar de Bandas 2026?

The 2026 edition moves to the Explanada del Monumento a la Revolución, located at Plaza de la República s/n in the Colonia Tabacalera neighbourhood of the Cuauhtémoc borough. The Revolución Metro station provides direct access.

Do you need tickets for Bazar de Bandas 2026?

No tickets are required. Admission is completely free for all attendees across all three days of the event.

World.title: Pinti Awards: All the Winners at the Colón Theater Honoring the Best of Commercial Theater
World.content:
Culture & Business

Key Facts —Ceremony. The first Pinti Awards gala was held at the Teatro Colón in Buenos Aires. —Top Winners. “Una Navidad de mierda” won Best Comedy and “Charlie y la fábrica de chocolate” won Best Musical. —Career Honours. Moria Casán, Guillermo Francella, and producer Carlos Rottemberg received lifetime achievement awards. —Organiser. The awards were created by AADET, the Argentine association of theatre producers. —Broadcast. The ceremony aired on eltrece and was hosted by actor Agustín “Rada” Aristarán.

The first Pinti Awards winners were crowned at Buenos Aires’s iconic Teatro Colón, with “Una Navidad de mierda” taking Best Comedy and veteran stars Moria Casán and Guillermo Francella receiving career honours, marking a new chapter for Argentina’s commercial theatre industry.

Pinti Awards: All the Winners at the Colón Theater Honoring the Best of Commercial Theater (Photo internet reproduction)

A New Prize for the Business of Theatre

The Pinti Awards, named after the late Argentine actor and comedian Enrique Pinti, arrived with a clear mission: to celebrate the commercial theatre that fills Buenos Aires’s famed Corrientes Avenue night after night. Created by AADET, the trade body representing theatre producers, the awards covered productions staged between August 2025 and June 2026.

Unlike state-subsidised festivals, these prizes focus squarely on the box office — the shows that draw paying audiences, employ large casts and crews, and generate tourism revenue. The choice of the Teatro Colón, Argentina’s most prestigious opera house, signalled the industry’s ambition to elevate commercial theatre to the same cultural standing as classical music and ballet.

The Night’s Big Winners

“Una Navidad de mierda,” an ensemble comedy led by Verónica Llinás, Alejo García Pintos, Tomás Fonzi, and Anita Gutiérrez, took the prize for Best Comedy. Llinás also won Best Actress in a Comedy for her performance in the same production.

In the musical categories, “Charlie y la fábrica de chocolate” — produced by the prolific Carlos Rottemberg and starring host Agustín “Rada” Aristarán — won Best Musical. Aristarán also collected the Best Actor in a Musical award, making him one of the evening’s most visible figures.

The Best Drama or Dramedy prize went to “Las hijas,” directed by Adrián Suar and starring Soledad Villamil, Florencia Peña, and Pilar Gamboa. “Rocky,” a stage adaptation of the boxing film, won the award for highest-attendance drama or dramedy, underlining its commercial pulling power.

Career Awards for Three Industry Pillars

The Pinti Awards dedicated a significant portion of the evening to lifetime achievement. Moria Casán, a vedette and actress whose career spans more than five decades, received the career award for female theatrical performance.

Guillermo Francella, one of Argentina’s most bankable film and television stars who has consistently returned to the stage, took the male acting career honour. Producer Carlos Rottemberg, whose family-run empire of theatres dominates the Corrientes strip, was recognised for his career in theatrical production.

These three figures represent the economic engine of Argentine show business. Rottemberg alone controls multiple venues and has produced hundreds of shows, while Francella and Casán are names that sell out houses within hours of tickets going on sale.

The Full List of Pinti Awards Winners

Across 19 competitive categories, the awards recognised acting, directing, design, and writing talent. “Lo que el río hace,” written by sisters María and Paula Marull, won Best Play by Argentine Authors, a category that highlights original local writing in a market often dominated by international adaptations.

Juan Pablo Geretto won Best Actor in a Comedy for “Berlín Berlín,” while Roberto Peloni took Best Actor in a Drama for “El brote.” Lorena Vega won Best Actress in a Drama for her work in “Imprenteros” and “La vida extraordinaria.”

In the technical categories, “Rocky” won for lighting, sound, and original music design by Mariano Demaría and Santiago Cámara. “Hairspray” collected two awards: costume and characterisation design for Gustavo Alderete, and choreography for Vanesa García Millán.

The audience favourite award, voted by the public, went to the classic musical “Annie.” “El jefe del jefe,” starring Diego Peretti and Federico D’Elía, was named Comedy of the Year. The unipersonal and alternative format prize went to “Suavecita.”

What the Pinti Awards Mean for Buenos Aires Theatre

Buenos Aires has long claimed one of the highest concentrations of theatres per capita in the world, with Corrientes Avenue functioning as its Broadway. The commercial theatre sector is a significant employer and a draw for domestic and regional tourism, particularly from Uruguay, Chile, and Brazil.

By creating an awards show specifically for commercial productions, AADET is building a brand that can market Argentine theatre internationally. The broadcast on eltrece, a major free-to-air network, guarantees visibility that can translate into ticket sales for winning shows.

For investors and expats, the Pinti Awards offer a snapshot of a resilient sector. Even as Argentina navigates economic volatility, theatre attendance remains a cultural constant, and productions that win awards often see extended runs and touring opportunities across Latin America.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the Pinti Awards?

The Pinti Awards are a new prize created by AADET, Argentina’s theatre producers’ association, to honour excellence in commercial theatre. Named after the late actor and comedian Enrique Pinti, the first ceremony was held at the Teatro Colón in Buenos Aires and covered productions staged between August 2025 and July 2026.

Who won the top prizes at the first Pinti Awards?

“Una Navidad de mierda” won Best Comedy, “Las hijas” won Best Drama or Dramedy, and “Charlie y la fábrica de chocolate” won Best Musical. Career awards went to actress Moria Casán, actor Guillermo Francella, and producer Carlos Rottemberg.

Why were the Pinti Awards created?

The awards were established to give commercial theatre in Argentina its own dedicated recognition, separate from state-funded or independent theatre prizes. The goal is to promote the industry, boost ticket sales, and strengthen Buenos Aires’s position as a leading theatre destination in Latin America.

Deborah Colker’s ‘Remix’ arrives at Belo Horizonte’s Sesc Palladium for a four-performance season starting 31 July 2026, bringing a bold reimagining of the company’s most celebrated works to Minas Gerais.

A Homecoming for Reinvented Classics

The Deborah Colker Companhia de Dança returns to Belo Horizonte with a production that mines its own history. ‘Remix’ is not a greatest-hits parade but a structural re-engineering of four landmark pieces.

The works span two decades of creation: *Vulcão* (1994), *Rota* (1997), *4×4* (2002), and *Belle* (2014). Each contributed a distinct physical vocabulary that helped define Colker’s international reputation.

The Deborah Colker Remix Concept

The company describes the production as its most ambitious recent undertaking. Rather than simply restaging old choreography, Colker has woven fragments into a two-act dramatic arc.

Audiences will recognise the famous hanging vases and the Ferris wheel apparatus. These objects, central to the original works, now serve a new narrative logic that connects the company’s past to its present.

Venue and Schedule at Sesc Palladium

The Grande Teatro do Sesc Palladium sits at Rua Rio de Janeiro, 1046, in Belo Horizonte’s city centre. It is the state’s premier receiving house for large-scale contemporary performance.

The season opens on Thursday, 31 July 2026, and continues with performances on Friday, 1 August, and Saturday, 2 August. An additional matinee has been confirmed for 1 August at 16:30, bringing the total to four shows.

What This Means for Brazil’s Cultural Economy

Colker’s company is one of Brazil’s most exportable cultural assets, having toured over 30 countries. A domestic tour of this scale signals confidence in the post-pandemic recovery of Brazil’s live-performance market.

For Belo Horizonte, hosting a high-profile national tour reinforces the city’s position as a secondary cultural hub. The Sesc Palladium run is likely to draw audiences from across Minas Gerais and neighbouring states.

The Investor and Expat Read-Through

Cultural infrastructure is a soft-power indicator that correlates with quality-of-life metrics for expatriates and relocating professionals. A city that can programme a company of Colker’s calibre demonstrates mature institutional capacity.

The production also highlights the resilience of Brazil’s creative industries, a sector that contributes meaningfully to GDP and urban regeneration. Sustained touring activity suggests stable consumer demand and functional arts funding mechanisms.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Deborah Colker’s ‘Remix’ about?

‘Remix’ is a two-act production that reinterprets four earlier works by the Deborah Colker Companhia de Dança: *Vulcão*, *Rota*, *4×4*, and *Belle*. It stitches iconic scenes into a new dramatic flow rather than presenting the original pieces unchanged.

When and where is ‘Remix’ showing in Belo Horizonte?

The production runs from 31 July to 2 August 2026 at the Grande Teatro do Sesc Palladium, located at Rua Rio de Janeiro, 1046, in the Centro district. There are four performances, including an extra matinee on 1 August at 16:30.

Which original works are featured in the ‘Remix’ production?

The show draws from *Vulcão* (1994), *Rota* (1997), *4×4* (2002), and *Belle* (2014). Audiences can expect to see famous set pieces such as the hanging vases and the Ferris wheel sequence recontextualised within the new work.

World.title: Bogotá Sacred Music Festival Turns 15 with Free Global Concerts

Culture & Frontier Living

Key Facts —Anniversary. The 2026 edition marks 15 years since the festival was founded in 2012. —Scale. Recent editions have featured over 750 artists from 16 countries across 40 events in 20 venues. —Access. Between 70 and 80 percent of all concerts are free to the public. —Recognition. The festival has been named an event of national interest by Colombia’s government and received royal honours from Spain. —Mission. It promotes interreligious dialogue and peace through sacred music from multiple faith traditions.

The Bogotá Sacred Music Festival reaches its 15th anniversary in 2026, consolidating the Colombian capital as a regional hub for large-scale sacred music performances that draw artists from across the globe and remain overwhelmingly free to the public.
