World.title: Powerful earthquake hits Japan, injuring at least 50
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaEarthquakes Powerful earthquake hits Japan, injuring at least 50 Anton Bridge and Mariko Katsumura July 28, 2026 — 10:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 7.1-magnitude earthquake hit Japan’s southern Kumamoto prefecture on Tuesday, knocking out power to thousands of homes, rupturing roads and leaving some trapped and others presumed dead inside a partially collapsed shopping mall. The tremor was centred around Kumamoto prefecture, about 900 km (560 miles) from central Tokyo, and hit at an extremely shallow depth of 10 km, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA). Aerial image showing the damaged AEON Mall after an earthquake in Kashima, Kumamoto prefecture, southern Japan. AP Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told media she had received some initial reports of injuries, while public broadcaster NHK reported that at least 50 people had been hurt. Speaking to reporters at her office in Tokyo, Takaichi said authorities were still assessing the full extent of the damage in the area, which was devastated by a deadly quake a decade ago.



“We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings,” she said. “I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location.” Around 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centres, the disaster management agency said, while Takaichi said 3,600 soldiers would be deployed to help with the disaster recovery as aftershocks continued to rumble. The quake’s maximum seismic intensity was estimated at 7 on a Japanese scale of 7. Shaking of that intensity makes it impossible to stand, according to the JMA. An initial quake just before 4:30pm Japan time was followed by a series of aftershocks in the same region.



One hospital had reported more than 50 injuries, public broadcaster NHK said. Several people on a high-speed train at the time of the quake were also injured, media reported. Multiple people were trapped inside an Aeon shopping mall rocked by an explosion that occurred after the earthquake, fire services said. Police said, “quite a few” were presumed dead in the incident, broadcaster TBS reported. An Aeon spokesperson said customers and employees were evacuated right after the initial quake and that the exact cause of the ensuing explosion was unclear. Kazuya Tsurunaga told TBS he heard the explosion while cleaning up dishes broken by the earthquake inside a pub about 300 metres from the Aeon mall.



“It was a huge impact,” he said. “A large cloud of smoke billowed up, and because the wind happened to be blowing and the wind direction was towards the shop, the area around us was in a state like volcanic ash was falling.” Rail operator JR Kyushu stopped all its services, while Kumamoto airport’s runway was closed for safety checks, with no time set for re-opening. Power outages were reported at some 7-Eleven stores in Kumamoto, while NTT Docomo experienced disruptions to mobile services. A store sign of a restaurant is seen fallen on the ground after an earthquake in Kumamoto in the Kyushu island, southern Japan, undefined/Kyodo News via AP No irregularities were reported at nuclear power facilities, chief cabinet secretary Minoru Kihara said. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing said it evacuated staff at its Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing facility. TSMC, the go-to chipmaker for Nvidia and Apple operates a factory in Kumamoto prefecture, with a second facility under construction.



Sony Group produces image sensors in Kyushu that are used in smartphones, while Tokyo Electron makes chip tools and advanced packaging equipment in the region. An aerial image shows part of a bridge that collapsed after the earthquake in Yatsushiro, Kumamoto prefecture, southern Japan. undefined/Kyodo News via AP Chip making in particular is highly sensitive to physical shocks or disruptions in power and processes, and minor hiccups can sometimes destroy whole batches of valuable product. Japan is one of the world’s most earthquake-prone countries, with a tremor occurring at least every five minutes. Located along the “Ring of Fire” of volcanoes and oceanic trenches partly encircling the Pacific Basin, Japan accounts for about 20 per cent of the world’s earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or more. A tsunami warning was issued immediately after Tuesday’s quake, but was later lifted.



Kyushu Electric Power said 48,000 homes had lost power as a result of the latest quake, while railway company JR Kyushu said that it had suspended services, including its high-speed bullet trains. A 6.5 magnitude earthquake in 2016 caused substantial damage to Kumamoto. Yusuke Ogata A massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and injured a further 2,739, according to an official count, and damaged thousands of buildings including the city’s castle, a top tourist site. Some portions of the stone walls at the castle also collapsed as a result of Tuesday’s quake, an official at the castle’s office said. While the federal government funding will not specifically target the top-flight Super Rugby Women’s, a beefed-up grassroots product shapes as a crucial building block towards growing the competition in the future. The Super Rugby Women’s season of just four rounds with a two-week finals system pales in comparison to countries such as England, where the Premiership Women’s Rugby is played over 20 weeks with nine teams. This has helped England feature in nine of 10 World Cup finals. The Wallaroos have not made it past the World Cup quarter-finals since 2010. Getty Images Rugby Australia has increased the Test program to at least 10 fixtures a year from 2026, but it has still grappled with player defections to the ever-growing NRLW, including Rugby 7s star Teagan Levi (Gold Coast Titans) and former Test squad member Caitlin Urwin (Brisbane Broncos).



The early program rollouts of the Australian Legacy funding into rugby have already generated an 8 per cent increase in female participation. Minister for Sport Anika Wells said a long-term legacy beyond the World Cup will be created from the initiative. Related Article Wallabies ‘Is this the end?’: Contract call twists fate for plagued Wallaby “The Albanese government’s $90 million investment will get more women, girls and grassroots players into rugby, growing the sport in Australia and the Pacific and leaving a lasting legacy from these major competitions,” Wells said. “The benefits of these tournaments will be felt well beyond the final whistle, encouraging Australians – especially women and girls – to pick up a ball and get involved.” The funding will also go towards women’s facility upgrades and the creation of courses to help more women and girls become coaches, referees and officials.



According to an AusPlay survey funded and led by the Australian Sports Commission, 39 per cent of Australians aged 15 and over who participated as a sports official in 2025 were women. However, that figure is not represented across the higher levels. Of the 44 clubs in the four women’s football codes – Super Rugby Women’s, NRLW, AFLW and A-League Women’s – only five head coaches are female: Karyn Murphy (Titans), Tamara Hyett (Western Bulldogs), Lisa Webb (Fremantle Dockers), Daisy Pearce (West Coast Eagles), and Natalie Wood (Essendon Bombers). Loading The federal government said the funding would also help deliver both Rugby World Cups – with the men’s 2027 showcase in Australia expected to generate more than $2 billion – while continuing to aid the Pacific Legacy program, which now operates in Fiji, Samoa and Tonga. “This is another way we are working with our Pacific neighbours to grow and strengthen our ties through sport,” Wells said. World.title: Why one of Australia’s largest childcare providers has banned school photos
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation Why one of Australia’s largest childcare providers has banned school photos Emily Kowal Updated July 28, 2026 — 10:21pm ,first published 7:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of Australia’s largest childcare providers has banned class photos, citing child safety concerns, leaving photography businesses scrambling and disappointed parents without the treasured keepsakes. Across the country, childcare centres are in a state of upheaval after a string of abuse incidents led to sweeping reforms banning staff from carrying mobile phones, smartwatches, tablets or any device capable of taking or transmitting images of children. It also created new rules on where photos and videos of children could be stored. Queensland mum Carrie said she was saddened when her children’s childcare stopped photos. For Goodstart Early Learning, which has more than 660 centres across Australia, the risk of photographs beyond its control being manipulated is too high at present. “Until we can be certain that every photography session is conducted by a photographer who has strict controls on the storage and security of photographs of children, we won’t be allowing commercial photography in our centres,” it said.



The phasing-out of traditional class photos comes at a time of growing debates and concern about the safety of children’s images. Schools have been warned it is no longer safe to share student’s images online as artificial intelligence becomes weaponised. Australian crime professor Michael Salter, an internationally recognised child sexual exploitation expert, said commercial photographers and childcare centres needed to change their practices. “The fact is that images of children, especially high-quality resolution images of children, now have an additional currency and valence they didn’t use to have,” Salter said. “It’s incumbent on parents to be very aware of the importance of preserving the privacy of their children. We are simply in an era where images and video is being scraped at scale. Internet service providers have not yet responded to the threat of this kind of data harvesting. “I think the photography industry and the education sector need to be alive to the risks and what minimum standards mean in this new environment.”



Related Article Exclusive

Education ‘No risk-free way’: Schools warned to stop posting student photos online While regulations do not prohibit commercial photography, many centres have come to the realisation that once the images are taken, they hand over control to photographers to store and process images safely. Queensland mum Carrie, who asked for her surname to be withheld, treasures the preschool photos of her children. But when she flicks to her son’s album, the pictures suddenly stop. “It came out of nowhere,” said Carrie. “Maybe in the big scheme of things, it is just a photo, but it is nostalgic to look back on. It’s almost a rite of passage,” she said. The decision shocked early childhood photographers, some of whom had been snapping photos at the centres for decades, and triggered a “mass wave of disruption and panic in the photography industry”, said Queensland photographer Liz Teece.



While current laws and regulations do not ban third-party school photos, they do not explicitly outline a standard policy or procedure. “Everyone is interpreting the Australian Children’s Education & Care Quality Authority regulations differently,” said Teece. “We have had mass revolt from parents who just want their child’s photo. It’s been incredibly tough to say to families we are sorry, but we just can’t.” Sydney photographer Clayton Walker has spent more than $50,000 updating his systems, having cybersecurity experts examine the software and training his staff in mandatory child protection issues. Families can log in and delete their own child’s photos at any time, even if the centre wants them active longer, and they do not keep images forever. Goodstart said it hoped to be able to reintroduce class photography in the future. “We are always exploring ways to improve our systems and practices and will be happy to reintroduce commercial class photography when we can assure ourselves that it is as safe as possible and meets the requirements of the national model code.”



“A lot of centres are making some pretty strong changes about their data and privacy policies and who they are allowing into the centre. It’s just created change, and there’s no particular one way that companies are doing it,” said Walker. He wishes the laws were clearer, as do other photographers, who have since formed an alliance, calling for official standards of consent, data security, child safety and professional conduct. Greens MLC Abigail Boyd, who chaired a parliamentary inquiry into Australia’s besieged childcare, sector said those in charge “still haven’t learnt the lesson”. “The teachers and educators I speak to are exasperated at failures in leadership in this sector. Not a single one of them has identified to me concerns about professional photographers taking photos with prudent and standard privacy and safety conditions.”



Mum Carrie said the decision was confusing, given many centres used apps to share photos of their children throughout the day. She worries that too will soon disappear. “I hate that I have to work and send my kids to day care, so it is nice to get those little updates,” said Carrie. World.title: Powerful earthquake hits Japan, injuring at least 50
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaEarthquakes Powerful earthquake hits Japan, injuring at least 50 Anton Bridge and Mariko Katsumura July 28, 2026 — 10:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 7.1-magnitude earthquake hit Japan’s southern Kumamoto prefecture on Tuesday, knocking out power to thousands of homes, rupturing roads and leaving some trapped and others presumed dead inside a partially collapsed shopping mall. The tremor was centred around Kumamoto prefecture, about 900 km (560 miles) from central Tokyo, and hit at an extremely shallow depth of 10 km, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA). Aerial image showing the damaged AEON Mall after an earthquake in Kashima, Kumamoto prefecture, southern Japan. AP Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told media she had received some initial reports of injuries, while public broadcaster NHK reported that at least 50 people had been hurt. Speaking to reporters at her office in Tokyo, Takaichi said authorities were still assessing the full extent of the damage in the area, which was devastated by a deadly quake a decade ago.



“We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings,” she said. “I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location.” Around 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centres, the disaster management agency said, while Takaichi said 3,600 soldiers would be deployed to help with the disaster recovery as aftershocks continued to rumble. The quake’s maximum seismic intensity was estimated at 7 on a Japanese scale of 7. Shaking of that intensity makes it impossible to stand, according to the JMA. An initial quake just before 4:30pm Japan time was followed by a series of aftershocks in the same region.



One hospital had reported more than 50 injuries, public broadcaster NHK said. Several people on a high-speed train at the time of the quake were also injured, media reported. Multiple people were trapped inside an Aeon shopping mall rocked by an explosion that occurred after the earthquake, fire services said. Police said, “quite a few” were presumed dead in the incident, broadcaster TBS reported. An Aeon spokesperson said customers and employees were evacuated right after the initial quake and that the exact cause of the ensuing explosion was unclear. Kazuya Tsurunaga told TBS he heard the explosion while cleaning up dishes broken by the earthquake inside a pub about 300 metres from the Aeon mall.



“It was a huge impact,” he said. “A large cloud of smoke billowed up, and because the wind happened to be blowing and the wind direction was towards the shop, the area around us was in a state like volcanic ash was falling.” Rail operator JR Kyushu stopped all its services, while Kumamoto airport’s runway was closed for safety checks, with no time set for re-opening. Power outages were reported at some 7-Eleven stores in Kumamoto, while NTT Docomo experienced disruptions to mobile services. A store sign of a restaurant is seen fallen on the ground after an earthquake in Kumamoto in the Kyushu island, southern Japan, undefined/Kyodo News via AP No irregularities were reported at nuclear power facilities, chief cabinet secretary Minoru Kihara said. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing said it evacuated staff at its Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing facility. TSMC, the go-to chipmaker for Nvidia and Apple operates a factory in Kumamoto prefecture, with a second facility under construction.



Sony Group produces image sensors in Kyushu that are used in smartphones, while Tokyo Electron makes chip tools and advanced packaging equipment in the region. An aerial image shows part of a bridge that collapsed after the earthquake in Yatsushiro, Kumamoto prefecture, southern Japan. undefined/Kyodo News via AP Chip making in particular is highly sensitive to physical shocks or disruptions in power and processes, and minor hiccups can sometimes destroy whole batches of valuable product. Japan is one of the world’s most earthquake-prone countries, with a tremor occurring at least every five minutes. Located along the “Ring of Fire” of volcanoes and oceanic trenches partly encircling the Pacific Basin, Japan accounts for about 20 per cent of the world’s earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or more. A tsunami warning was issued immediately after Tuesday’s quake, but was later lifted.



Kyushu Electric Power said 48,000 homes had lost power as a result of the latest quake, while railway company JR Kyushu said that it had suspended services, including its high-speed bullet trains. A 6.5 magnitude earthquake in 2016 caused substantial damage to Kumamoto. Yusuke Ogata A massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and injured a further 2,739, according to an official count, and damaged thousands of buildings including the city’s castle, a top tourist site. Some portions of the stone walls at the castle also collapsed as a result of Tuesday’s quake, an official at the castle’s office said. Reuters, with Bloomberg Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: The week in Parliament : A new watcher of judges and a free-for-all debate on petitions
World.content:
Highlights for the coming week in Parliament include a new judge watcher, a large group of visiting female Pacifica MPs, a Privileges Committee hearing into MBIE staff, and a free-for-all debate on petitions. Also, a briefing on bird flu and, of course, a bevy of bills up for debate.

A Privileges hearing into MBIE immigration

On Tuesday evening Parliament's Privileges Committee begins hearings into whether MBIE's Immigration leadership misled a Select Committee over the status and success of a failed IT upgrade project.

When Parliament's rights and responsibilities (i.e. Privileges) may have been contravened, complaints are first made to the sitting Speaker. If the Speaker believes there is a potential 'matter of privilege' it is referred to the Privileges Committee, a cross-party committee of senior MPs who hold hearings and make a recommendation to the House.

The hearing is from 5-6pm this evening.

A new watcher for the judges

Early business from MPs on Tuesday was a short debate on a motion that the House recommend that the Governor General appoint Paul Norman Collins as Judicial Conduct Commissioner for a term of 5 years, under section 7(2) of the Judicial Conduct Commissioner and Judicial Conduct Panel Act 2004.

The Attorney General noted that The Chief Justice had been consulted as required. Only National, Labour and Green MPs spoke on the motion and all agreed.

Parliament has sovereignty among the three branches of government (the Legislature, the Executive, the Judiciary), but a key constitutional principle in the relationship that the Executive and Legislature have with the judiciary is "comity". A mutual respect and restraint, recognising one another's independence. This is why it is very poor form for an MP or minister to criticise a judge or judicial decision.

To maintain judicial independence there is an independent overseer of judicial conduct. The role does not review decisions. This helps to keep politicians from muddying comity's limpid waters.

Female MPs in the Fale

Pacifica women MPs are visiting New Zealand's Parliament this week as part of the Tai a Kiwa: Stronger Pacific Parliament's programme. This week's programme includes female MPs from across the Pacific and will discuss issues of common interest; including Leading Effectively in Male-dominated Environments, featuring General Rose King (New Zealand's Chief of Army) and Cushla Tangaere-Manuel (MP for Ikaroa-Rāwhiti, Labour; and former chief executive of the Ngāti Porou East Coast Rugby Union).

Depressingly, another session covers Online Harm & Gender-Based Harassment and features Nicola Grigg (Minister for Women's Affairs), Carmel Sepuloni (Deputy Leader of Labour), Tamatha Paul (Green MP for Wellington Central), and Hana-Rāwhiti Maipi-Clarke (MP for Hauraki-Waikato, Te Pāti Māori).

A petition free-for-all

At noon on Wednesday MPs will spend an hour debating everything any Kiwi has complained about. Well, almost. This doesn't include complaints over a beer at the pub. It is a debate about anything that has been raised in a formal petition to Parliament. But that is still a lot of things. This Tuesday alone Parliament received the following five petitions:

Petition of Hannah McKeich requesting that the House make childcare screening mandatory for parents before scheduled surgery or in cases of emergency hospitalisation.

Petition of Pegasus Residents Group requesting that the House urge the Government to ensure that the proposal to redevelop the Pegasus Golf Course is not progressed through the fast-track approvals process.

Petition of Andreas Fox requesting that the House amend the definition of rape in the Crimes Act 1961 so that rape does not require the perpetrator to have a penis.

Petition of Sheryl Tristram requesting that the House suspend the provisions of section 23(4) of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, where these relate to persons charged with offences against children.

Petition of Tracey McLeod requesting that the House investigate funding for the Rotorua Lakes sewerage schemes and the Rotorua Te Arawa Lakes strategy.

A bird flu briefing

Often when a new biosecurity threat arrives in New Zealand there is a ministerial briefing to the House on the issue, outlining the response that is planned. Thus far, the recent detection of H5N1 has not provoked a briefing.

For those wanting an update on what could be an avian catastrophe in a country where many bird species are threatened (without even touching on commercial bird raising for eggs or meat).

A briefing is scheduled to the Primary Industry Committee at 10am on Thursday morning. The briefing is coming from biosecurity staff from both the Department of Conservation and the Ministry for Primary Industries.

Four laws up for finalising

Among the bills being debated in the House this week, the government is hoping to finalize four that the House also spent time on last week.

The Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill is written to ease the use of Special Purpose Vehicles, entities created to fund and build infrastructure at a remove from a Local Council's balance sheets; and to repay their financing by charging levies to those benefited by the infrastructure, for up to 50 years. The ongoing liability for levies would be added to a property's LIM. This bill has now passed its third and final reading leaving only final confirmations and assent from the Crown.

The Employment Leave Bill would replace the Holidays Act 2003, which has long caused confusion. There is wide agreement that it could be improved, but less agreement over whether this bill will fix the issue. This is a tough area to get right when it must cover full time, part-time, variable hours, shifts, contracts, and casual workers. The plan is for a Committee stage on Tuesday and third reading on Wednesday.

The English Language Bill is, at its core, just eight words long. It doesn't change anything, but confirms that "English is an official language of New Zealand." Legal scholars will tell you that this is already the case - otherwise it would be a problem that this bill is written in English.

The Arms Bill slightly alters a few aspects of weapon regulation. Major changes include removing the arms regulator role from the Police, introducing new licence types for museum employees, and new rules for who can use restricted types of weapons for pest control.

Other bills slated for debate this week are the Crimes Amendment Bill, the Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill, the Building and Construction (Strengthening Occupational Licensing Regimes) Amendment Bill, and the Commerce (Promoting Competition and Other Matters) Amendment Bill.

World.title: MBIE chief denies attempt to mislead Parliament over failed $35m project
World.content:
The chief executive of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment has accepted the ministry got things wrong when it did not disclose information to MPs about a cancelled IT project earlier this year.

But he denies the ministry deliberately attempted to mislead Parliament.

In March, MBIE failed to tell Parliament's Education and Workforce Committee that the $35 million Biometric Capability Update (BCU) project had been axed, telling MPs there was no public review about its progress.

In reality, the project was already dead.

In June, Speaker Gerry Brownlee referred the matter to the Privileges Committee, after Labour's Phil Twyford and the Education and Workforce Committee both raised it as a matter of privilege.

MBIE chief executive Nic Blakeley appearing before the Privileges Committee. Giles Dexter / RNZ

Appearing before the Privileges Committee on Tuesday evening, MBIE chief executive Nic Blakeley said the ministry had a "genuinely held belief" that there were Budget and commercial sensitivities limiting what it could say in a public forum.

"In hindsight, we should have taken a different approach."

Committee chair Chris Bishop asked why, when asked in March about the key risks and milestones in the project's implementation, Blakeley could not simply say it had been terminated.

"I agree. We got it wrong. I accept that and we should have said differently," Blakeley said.

He added MBIE was still in negotiations over a final payment to Japanese tech company NEC over the project at the time, and so it was concerned that talking about it publicly would make it difficult to conclude those negotiations.

He also accepted MBIE could have gone into a "secret hearing" with the public removed from the committee room.

The decision not to talk about it was not an active decision, he insisted, but more an understanding between himself and Immigration New Zealand's then-boss Alison McDonald that there were sensitivities that limited what they could say.

Blakeley acknowledged that too was a failing.

MBIE chief executive Nic Blakeley, and the now retired head of INZ Alison McDonald, at select committee in March 2026. Screenshot / New Zealand Parliament

National's Scott Simpson said given Twyford had been asking questions and filing Official Information Act requests before the meeting, it should have been a sufficient flag.

"I agree with you," Blakeley replied.

"It's surprising, in hindsight, that there's no written material on BCU that shows that we weren't well enough prepared, and I accept that."

ACT's Parmjeet Parmar asked Blakeley whether he was happy with the information the ministry had provided.

"At the time, I didn't think I was doing anything wrong. I thought I was answering the questions as best I could, given the limitations that we had."

Parmar also questioned whether there were discussions after the hearing in March about what was said.

"We felt that we'd raised the questions as best we could, given the limitations we were under," Blakeley replied.

National's Chris Bishop. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

An audibly and visibly frustrated Bishop said the entire situation "beggars belief".

"The project was a disaster. The fact that no-one bothered to prepare to explain why it was a disaster, that's both terrible and good for you, bad for the public service," Bishop told Blakeley.

Blakeley would not answer questions from media following the hearing, saying he would wait for the Committee's findings.

Appearing via Zoom from the United Kingdom, the now-retired McDonald said in her mind, the programme had not stopped.

"It hadn't stopped. It had carried on going. The IT project was one element of the identity programme and we had done a lot of preparation around our future services, which is the big IT overhaul piece, if you like, for Immigration New Zealand.

"The biometric capability IT project wasn't managed by me or Immigration New Zealand. It was managed by another part of MBIE."

Bishop asked why McDonald was fronting on it if Immigration New Zealand had nothing to do with it.

McDonald explained the deputy secretary responsible had just resigned and Blakeley had only just started in an acting capacity.

"I honestly thought I was trying to help the committee understand that we were moving in a different direction. On reflection, that was the wrong thing to do."

She accepted that when Tywford was asking about milestones, she should have "paused a bit" and realised he was asking about the IT project specifically, rather than the wider work programme.

"I had no intention whatsoever to mislead the select committee and I find the suggestion that I might have acted deliberately to mislead Parliament extremely distressing," she said.

Education Minister Erica Stanford. RNZ / Louis Dunham

Immigration minister Erica Stanford has accused the ministry of deliberately witholding information from her and the previous Labour government about the project.

On Tuesday morning, Stanford would not presuppose what happened in the hearing.

World.title: Man accused of threatening to carry out attacks on two Auckland schools
World.content:
A man accused of threatening to carry out attacks on two Auckland schools and destroy public buildings allegedly said that he wanted to kill more people than the Christchurch mosque terrorist.

Tiedan Huo is on trial in the Manukau District Court, facing a raft of charges relating to a manifesto he allegedly distributed threatening to kill people at Waiuku and Rutherford colleges. He also allegedly threatened to destroy or damage two police stations and buildings at Parliament.

The man has also been charged with unlawful possession of a firearm, unlawful possession of explosives and possession of objectionable material.

Huo denies all the charges.

In his opening address to the jury, Crown prosecutor Gareth Kayes said that on 12 March last year, staff at Waiuku College woke to a chilling email that had been sent at 1:42am.

"It was titled 'Important: Don't come to school tomorrow'. And it started with the words 'This is my manifesto'."

Man accused of threatening to attack two Auckland schools Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

The email spoke of being bullied and humiliated by teachers at the school, being unfairly treated by police and being made to feel like a second-class citizen for being Chinese.

"I am going to do something about this now. I have began [sic] preparing for doing something about this since February this year and have finished now."

The email went on to set out in some detail the preparations the sender said they'd made to carry out attacks on Waiuku and Rutherford colleges, as well as damaging the Pukekohe and Te Atatu police stations and buildings at Parliament.

That included making firearms using a 3D printer and creating bullets and explosives to be used in an attack.

The sender said they wanted to kill more people than the Christchurch mosque terrorist, who murdered 51 innocent people on March 15, 2019.

"Do not assume that my guns will not work or are fake because they are 3D printed, that will be very bad."

The email was purportedly sent by a female former Waiuku College student, but after she allowed police to examine her electronic devices, officers established this was not the case, and their inquiries led them to Huo.

The threatening email was sent via an encrypted service but police found a screenshot on Huo's laptop captured just minutes after it was sent, showing the same username as the email.

"There were also a hundred used shotgun shells and a large knife," Kayes told the jury.

"Mr Huo's mother had a second address where Mr Huo would also stay ... In Mr Huo's bedroom at that address police found a loaded pump-action shotgun."

DNA analysis of the firearm found it was 90 billion times more likely to have come from Huo than anyone else.

His mother held a valid firearms licence and a second shotgun was found locked up in a gun safe at her home. Huo has not been charged in relation to that weapon.

Kayes said police found numerous manifestos and videos from mass shooters and terrorists, including the video taken by the Christchurch terrorist.

"These are all what's called, legally, 'objectionable publications'," Kayes told the jury.

"You might be relieved to hear you won't need to view them as part of this trial. That's because they've already all been classified as objectionable by the New Zealand Classifications Office."

What the jury would have to determine, the prosecutor said, was whether Huo did have the publications in his possession. It was the same question they must ask regarding the firearms and explosives charges, he said.

"I suggest that once you have heard all the evidence you will be left in no doubt that it was Mr Huo who sent the manifesto."

The Crown's first witness, Waiuku College principal Stuart Kelly, was asked about the process of putting the school into lockdown after the email was received.

He said the school had taken the threat "very, very seriously".

World.title: A delayed flu season could be on the way as winter ills and chills hit
World.content:
Dr Mamaeroa David on protecting against winter illness Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Winter ills and chills are upon us, but while there are plenty of viruses going around, a health modeller says the flu season is yet to peak.

University of Canterbury mathematical modeller, Professor Michael Plank, said we were in the middle of the winter respiratory season, which was about normal for the time of year, but rates of influenza remained low.

It seemed there was either a small flu season this year, or a late one, Plank said, with the possibility of more illness yet to come.

In 2025, New Zealand had an extended, late flu season, Plank said with cases going through to December due to a new variant of influenza, which prolonged the season.

Michael Plank. (File photo)

"It could mean we see a delayed flu season or smaller flu season this winter. There's a similar pattern in Australia as well.

"Influenza rates there have increased noticeably in the last couple of weeks and there are signs it might be starting to uptick here as well."

Plank said the start of the flu season could be soon, with a peak to come in the next month.

Cases of Covid-19 were also relatively low at present, Plank said, noting it was less seasonal than other viruses and could be a "little all over the place".

"Covid is at very low levels really, looking at the wastewater data, and hospital admissions [for Covid-19] were also very low at the moment."

RSV, Respiratory syncytial virus, was probably at its peak, Plank said, and there were various other viruses around causing similar cough and cold symptoms.

His advice was anyone who was ill should stay at home and keep up to date with vaccinations.

It was certainly not too late to get a flu vaccination, Plank said, as if a late flu season did begin, anyone newly vaccinated would gave high levels of immunity.

He also urged people to stay up to date with Covid boosters.

Senior Māori Medical Advisor with the Immunisation Advisory and Auckland GP, Dr Mamaeroa David, told Morning Report cold viruses were chugging along as well as RSV.

"I feel like we're getting one illness, getting knocked back, going back to kindy or work and getting the next bout of germs," she said.

She said if people could afford it, RAT testing for Covid, influenza and RSV could be useful to let people know what they had - especially since most GPs had a two to three week wait for appointments.

Covid-19 RAT tests. (File photo) AFP

"If you know what you've got, you may not need to see a GP."

Flu vaccination rates were lagging, she said, but as flu season hadn't fully kicked in yet, she agreed there was still time to be immunised.

"Flu vaccination is funded for over 65s and people with other co-morbidities, but if it's not funded for you, most places, like Chemist Warehouse can give you the vaccine for about $24.

"The flu hasn't hit yet but it is coming."

Auckland school feeling the strain

At Glenbrook School in rural South Auckland, principal Lysandra Stuart said winter illnesses were having a large impact on learning with high levels of absenteeism from students and staff.

"We're probably seeing a little bit more than we would typically see at this time of year. If you're a parent and a staff memver you get the double whammy of your students and your children getting sick."

Classes were being impacted by sickness. (File photo) Unsplash

Last week, the first week back of term, Stuart said she had three staff off and and this week she already had to drop tools and get into the classroom to cover classes.

She said one day she had five classes in the school hall with her.

"We're seeing it with our working parents too... kids come back with a sniff or cough too early."

Stuart believe that could be down to pressures around attendance.

She said there were days where 50 to 60 percent of a class were away.

Brining in relievers could be "horrendously costly", she said, so her school often looked at splitting or doubling classes when teachers were away.

In a worst case scenario, Stuart said parents were asked to help out.

Her advice to parents was the "usual stuff", she said, including having a good routine around sleep, eating well if possible and looking after hygiene.

"If you need to stay home please do, because we don't want others getting sick."

The Ministry of Education's Helen Hurst, said the ministry was not aware of any widespread national staffing disruption across schools.

"Just like in the wider population, schools typically experience higher levels of illness during the winter months, and some schools may face temporary challenges managing staff and student absences."

She said schools had well established processes for managing illness and infectious diseases including accessing relief staff, adjusting operational arrangements and working with Health NZ and public health officials.

"We continue to encourage schools and families to follow health guidance on when children should stay home and when they are well enough to attend school."

Advice for businesses

The Employers and Manufacturers Association's (EMA) head of advocacy Alan McDonald said he hadn't heard of any major disruption to workplaces due to illness this winter.

He said sickness at work hit each business differently, and the answer could sometimes be getting in a contractor to help or having to rely on other people doing a little bit extra.

"Generally employers are much more... they recognise sickness in the workplace as something they need to manage well. The days of 'oh I've got a head cold, I feel a bit miserable, but I'll come into the office', that's over.

"If Covid taught us anything it's that if people are sick in the workplace you don't want them coming in, you don't want them infecting other people, so generally the best management is to tell them to stay home."

McDonald said this is what the EMA told its employees.

World.title: Amorangi summit returns to promote tikanga-led governance
World.content:
Amorangi, the biennial Māori in Governance Summit, returns to Wellington on Wednesday, aiming to give Māori and non-Māori governors an understanding of tikanga-led governance.

This year's programme features 10 speakers from across the governance spectrum, including Te Pāti Māori MP Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke, Waitangi Tribunal Chair Chief Judge Caren Fox, Deputy Vice-Chancellor Māori and Kaitiakitanga Rawinia Higgins, and Wellington Rugby Director Erin Roxburgh.

Tapuwae Roa Kaihautū and Labour party candidate Te Pūoho Kātene (Ngāti Toarangatira, Ngāti Whātua, Ngāti Tama) told RNZ Amorangi was created to form a connected community for people involved in governance throughout Te Ao Māori.

He said there was increasing demand for governance development from a tikanga Māori lens, and not just from Māori authorities.

"On Māori boards, what we are seeing more and more is that we want to maintain and paddle our own waka. And so having to appoint boards that can do both in terms of stepping into the tikanga place, stepping into the mātauranga place, but also being effective and astute governors at the same time and not having to feel like you need to sacrifice one in order to prop the other one up.

"And I think what we've understood is that these aren't perfect circles of a Venn diagram, there are overlaps. And so we will take parts of tikanga and mātauranga that apply, but we'll never assume that authority transfers from one world to the other, because in the end, they're their own whare or their own discipline."

Amorangi is hosted by Tapuwae Roa, the pan-Māori charitable trust established by the Māori Fisheries Act in 2005, to pursue tikanga-led social change via targeted funding, investment and delivery of impactful kaupapa.

Karen Vercoe (front), Bayden Barber (centre), and Atawhai Tibble (back) on stage at Amorangi: Māori in Governance Summit 2024. Supplied/Tapuwae Roa

Kātene said practicing tikanga-led governance while working on Māori boards required finding a way to walk between both Māori and Pākehā worlds and at times bring those two worlds together.

"There's a focus heavily on mandate and the importance of understanding from whence your mandate comes and making sure that whoever gives it to you, whether it's your iwi members, whether it's your appointing body, whether it's your shareholders, that you, in that spot, are earning that mandate. I often like to say that mandate isn't owned, it's leased, and rent is due every day."

Katene said those in positions of power and decision-making authority need to make sure they are cognizant of who gave them that mana.

Thinking of governance through a lens of tikanga could also help people work through systems where they are incentivised to think short-term, he said.

"It gives us another viewpoint particularly to unpick any biases towards recency or towards short-termism. Tikanga is a really good foil to make sure we're making decisions with people at its heart and also with future generations in mind."

The surging Maori economy Nine To Noon Download MP3 31m

In 2024 Amorangi expanded to a hybrid model with both in-person and virtual attendance.

Kātene said this year in-person attendance had sold out, with more than 450 people expected to attend in person, and around 800 participants expected overall.

He said Amorangi was created with a focus on accessibility, so it would be open to professional governors as well people on marae committees, iwi trusts and businesses.

"That rounded, diverse range of perspectives that we bring in, as well as opening the gate, makes this much greater than another event. I think it's something that we can look around to our Māori at the moment and celebrate what makes us special and what value we can add into these spaces, not just for our organisation, but for the wider community."

World.title: Investigation launched after pōhutukawa trees poisoned
World.content:
Two pōhutukawa trees have been illegally poisoned in the Coromandel, the Department of Conservation says.

There was clear evidence of drill holes around the base of the trees at Hahei Beach Marginal Strip, Hauraki-Coromandel DoC staff wrote in a post on Facebook.

An investigation was underway.

A drill hole at the bottom of one of the trees. Department of Conservation - Hauraki-Coromandel

"Pōhutukawa are iconic coastal trees, often celebrated as Aotearoa's unofficial Christmas tree. But they are much more than a beautiful part of our summer landscape, they are important coastal ecosystems in their own right.

"Their flowers provide nectar for tūī, bellbirds and geckos, while their trunks, bark and canopy offer habitat for birds, insects and spiders. A diverse community of native insects depends on pōhutukawa, and the leaf litter beneath them supports hardy native snails adapted to life along the coast. Shags and white-faced herons often nest or roost in pōhutukawa," staff wrote.

Two pōhutukawa trees at Hahei Beach in the Coromandel have been illegally poisoned. Supplied

The trees' root systems helped to stabilise coastal soils, dunes and cliffs.

Damaging, poisoning or destroying native vegetation on public conservation land is a serious offence, which can result in penalties including fines of up to $300,000.

DoC staff are asking anyone with information about who may be responsible to contact them and quote the reference number: CLE-12213.

World.title: Joint spares Aussie blushes on tough day at Memphis Open
World.content:
Rising star Maya Joint has spared Australia's blushes at the WTA's hard-court event in Memphis.

On a day when the Australian challenge fizzled, the world number 77 won her round-of-16 clash against wildcard Whitney Osuigwe in straight sets.

The 20-year-old needed a tick over 90 minutes for a 6-4, 6-1 win against the American.

Joint will now meet the winner of top-seed Ekaterina Alexandrova or fellow Russian Kristina Liutova for a place in the quarterfinals.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Already boasting tournament victories in Rabat and Eastbourne last year, which helped her climb to a career-best number 28 in the world in February this year, Joint lost her serve twice in the opening set but did enough to take it in 45 minutes.

The second set proved more comfortable and Joint, who famously eliminated Serena Williams in the opening round of Wimbledon this year, broke three times to advance.

There was no such joy for Talia Gibson and Storm Hunter though.

Gibson was soundly beaten by German Tatjana Maria 6-0, 6-3, while compatriot Storm Hunter succumbed 7-5, 7-5 to fifth-seeded Colombian Camila Osorio.

World number 66 Kimberly Birrell, who lost her first-round doubles clash alongside American Peyton Stearns to Ingrid Martins and Ekaterina Ovcharenko 6-4, 6-7 (7/4), 11-9, takes on China's Ma Yexin in the singles draw on Tuesday.

In the shock of the day, Swiss third seed Viktorija Golubic was eliminated in three sets by Katie Volynets of the US, while all three unseeded Russian players in action were victorious.

World.title: Embattled LIV Golf tour asks to defer payment to Adelaide golf club
World.content:
The financially struggling LIV Golf tour has asked for an extension on a payment to Kooyonga Golf Club, raising doubts over whether next year's Adelaide event will go ahead.

Kooyonga in Adelaide's western suburbs is scheduled to host LIV Golf Adelaide in 2027 before the tour moves to a newly redeveloped North Adelaide Golf Course in 2028.

But the future of the league has been under a cloud since Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) announced it would be pulling its reported billions in funding at the end of the 2026 season.

The Grange Golf Club has previously hosted the LIV event in Adelaide. (ABC News: Rory McClaren)

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas said he was made aware last week that LIV Golf had asked for an extension on a payment to Kooyonga Golf Club.

"An extension was sought by LIV as they're working through programming next year for those payments to be made in September," he said.

"That extension was granted."

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas says he is aware LIV Golf has asked for an extension. (ABC News)

Mr Malinauskas indicated there would "presumably" be enough time for Kooyonga to prepare for the March 2027 event, given the club had granted the payment extension.

The deferred payment is worth $500,000, Adelaide radio station FIVEaa reported.

In a statement, Kooyonga Golf Club confirmed it "evaluated and approved" a "short operational extension regarding its initial venue payment" to LIV Golf.

Deputy Liberal leader Josh Teague said the government needed to be more transparent about the event's future.

SA's deputy Liberal leader Josh Teague wants more transparency about the event's future. (ABC News: Olivia Mason)

"Those who've bought tickets, those who are committing all sorts of other ways to the holding of the event are going to be left mightily disappointed … if all of a sudden LIV Golf goes from hero to zero," he said.

"If there's one thing you need to host successful international events, it's confidence and it's the capacity for everybody to get behind something because you know that it's actually going to happen and not just be shrouded in doubt.

"That's unfortunately where we stand right now."

The ABC has contacted LIV Golf for comment.

The shift to North Adelaide has been controversial. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The premier has previously said the state government would need a "clear indication" from LIV Golf about the event's future by October.

Can the SA government justify a $45m golf course upgrade without LIV Golf? The Malinauskas government took a calculated risk to redevelop the North Adelaide Golf Course in time for LIV Golf in 2028. It might not pay off.

The state government has a contract with LIV Golf until 2031 and pays an undisclosed fee for the tour to host an annual event in Adelaide.

LIV Golf's success at the Grange Golf Club was also the catalyst for the government to fund a controversial $45 million redevelopment of the North Adelaide Golf Course.

The project has been subject to protests over the felling of 585 trees.

The government has since secured the Australian Open golf tournament to be hosted at the North Adelaide Golf Course from 2028 to 2034.

World.title: The sun has set on the British Empire, and yet this celebration remains
World.content:
"It's just a square."

That's the three-star review of Nelson Mandela Place in Glasgow by someone named Katie Nicholson on Google.

Katie isn't entirely wrong. A statue for the freedom fighter and former South African president is set to be unveiled in October, but for now there's not a whole lot to see at the spot, listed as a tourist attraction on Google Maps.

But the couple of street signs tacked to buildings on West George Street, not far from the city centre, sit as an elegant and understated middle finger to apartheid South Africa.

The South African consulate left this location for some reason. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

In 1986, while Mandela was still in prison on Robben Island, the Glasgow City Council changed the name of St George's Place to Nelson Mandela Place.

It meant that the South African consulate under the then-ruling National Party was forced not only to see the name of one of their chief antagonists as they entered the Stock Exchange building every day, but also send out correspondence bearing his name.

They opted to use a PO Box address before moving from the location in the early 90s.

After Mandela was released, he came to the city to thank the people for their solidarity in 1993.

Nelson Mandela thanked Glasgow in 1993, between being released from prison and becoming president of South Africa. (Getty Images: Chris Bacon/PA)

"While we were physically denied our freedom in the country of our birth, a city 6,000 miles away, and as renowned as Glasgow, refused to accept the legitimacy of the apartheid system, and declared us to be free."

That cry of freedom is as synonymous with the Scottish as it is with Mandela himself.

So, how does a celebration of this Commonwealth sit with a city and country that has always had a fraught relationship with oppressors generally and the English specifically?

ABE – Anyone but England

Andy Murray got to represent Scotland in the 2022 Battle of the Brits. (Getty Images: Mark Runnacles/Battle of the Brits)

Tennis great Andy Murray once perplexed some (read: Americans) less au fait with the unique rivalries within the UK when he was asked who he'd be supporting at the 2006 FIFA World Cup and replied: "Anyone but England."

Scotland isn't on its own in this regard.

In the Ashes last summer, Australia's injury-plagued men's Test team scored a triumphant professional 4-1 victory, but more Australian joy was derived from watching another epic capitulation of an England team that had declared itself the saviour of Test cricket, teaching us all how to entertain, if not actually win much of anything.

We cheered every humiliating faceplant and fumble at least as much as we celebrated the all-time world-class performances of Travis Head and Mitchell Starc.

The recently completed World Cup was another reminder of the collective glee shared by so many in watching England stumble.

The Sun has set on the British Empire, and yet this celebration remains. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

There's just something about the schadenfreude for Scots, Aussies and dozens of other nations in watching England lose.

Sure, you've got the Parthenon Sculptures and Rosetta Stone, but we've got Ellyse Perry and Steve Smith.

"There is this standard, reflexive idea of that they would prefer almost everybody to win other than England, as the most powerful part of the United Kingdom," Western Sydney University emeritus professor of culture and research David Rowe told ABC Sport.

"I think for some people it's serious, for some people it's just a bit of fun."

Loading Instagram content

There are jokes to be made, but also reflections on the very real subjugation that went on for centuries, and arguably only ended in 1997 when Hong Kong gained its independence.

This celebration of empire remains a peculiarity as calls grow to decolonise our language and our lives.

For a perfect example, the Parthenon Sculptures mentioned earlier are more famously known as the Elgin Marbles, named for the lord who nicked them from Greece and brought them back to Old Blighty at the start of the 19th century.

"I mean, the Commonwealth of Nations is, let's face it, anachronistic," Rowe said.

Flags that don't always get to fly wave prominently at the Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"There are people who … don't know much about it or, if they schooled up on it, educated themselves about it, would realise that this is an anachronistic organisation based on an empire that no longer technically exists."

Although, many in the still-constituent Scotland would tell you the legacy, if not the actuality, of the empire remains in many ways.

"There are plenty of people in Scotland, including its leading Scottish National Party, who really would prefer to separate from the United Kingdom and who are mightily displeased by Brexit," said Rowe, a sports sociologist who consulted on the Glasgow Life team tasked with helping boost the city's standing on the global sporting stage.

"There are plenty of Scots who felt a greater affinity with the European Union than with England."

Strange, anomalous and anachronistic

A time machine is perhaps a fitting vehicle of entry of an event harking back to the past. (AAP: Andrew Milligan/PA Wire)

At the opening ceremony of the 2026 Commonwealth Games, King Charles III and Queen Camilla were warmly welcomed by the packed crowd at Glasgow's Hydro, perhaps surprisingly considering the same crowd's hearty refrains of Flower of Scotland barely an hour later.

The Scottish anthem retells Robert the Bruce's legendary victory over King Edward II of England at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314.

The thrust of the rousing choon, and Scotland's identity more broadly, is about how this small but mighty land of hard folk repelled the crown time and again on the back of sheer grit and pride.

So ingrained in their identity is sticking it to the English that, instead of tearing down statues of old royals and dignitaries like the Duke of Wellington, they have simply given up on removing the traffic cones placed on his head.

The Games have never opened like this – maybe they always should The 2026 Commonwealth Games are like no other that came before them and the opening ceremony was similarly unique in a way that will make it hard to go back.

And yet, twice in the past 12 years, Glasgow has gone out of its way to host what is correctly dubbed the Friendly Games, welcoming dozens of nations whose primary unifying theme is that they were once conquered by the "bastards" from that anthem.

"It does strike me as something of an irony that it's not that very long ago that Scotland had a referendum to sever its ties with the United Kingdom and the British Crown, and now it's hosting a Commonwealth Games," Rowe said.

"I think it's having a bit of fun, all the kilts and all the Scottish culture, reminding people that Scotland has its own identity and has not just been subsumed by the United Kingdom."

The Commonwealth Games has the royal seal of approval. (Getty Images: Aaron Chown/WPA Pool)

If you need more evidence of the strange bedfellows in effect, Rowe said you need only look at the event's original name.

It was called the British Empire Games from 1930 to 1950, the British Empire and Commonwealth Games until for the next four editions, and the British Commonwealth Games until 1972.

"So even more coded British," Rowe told ABC Sport.

"And it's a strange body in some ways, if you consider that it is a monument to colonialism and imperialism. And yet the members, most of whom were formerly under the jurisdiction of the British crown, were colonised, have now voluntarily agreed to join an organisation which was formed out of that imperial arrangement."

It also provides those in the British Isles a chance to beat England while representing Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, Guernsey, Jersey or the Isle of Man.

Scottish knights of the British Empire Chris Hoy and Andy Murray have won a combined 13 Olympic medals for Great Britain.

Duncan Scott is Team GB's most decorated Olympic swimmer, Mark Cavendish has won a world championship and Olympic silver with the Union Jack next to his name, but both turned around to beat the English while flying the Scottish saltire and Isle of Man's triskelion during the Commonwealth Games.

Duncan Scott has won more Olympic medals than any other British swimmer. (Supplied: Commonwealth Sport)

So how does the home crowd feel watching their sporting heroes flying those flags?

"I think it means more to them to compete for Scotland," one Glasgow local, Peter, told ABC Sport.

"You can see it in their faces when they do better. It does mean a lot more to them to represent their home country."

There's perhaps a hint of personal projection in this fan's assessment, as summed up by his mate, Pat.

"I would hope that it does [mean more] for them, because it would for me," he said.

Duncan Scott with the 2014 and 2026 mascots, the latter sporting a traffic cone for a horn. (Getty Images: Jane Barlow/PA Images)

No amount of raucous crowd support or national pride is going to turn a 45-year-old bricklayer who's had a hot dog for breakfast into a 10-flat 100m runner. But at the tippy-top of sport, where the margins are at their finest, it's got to be worth a few hundredths of a second.

Angharad Evans swam for Team GB at the 2025 world championships in Singapore, missing the semifinals and finishing a brutal 18th overall in the 100m breaststroke as she went almost two seconds slower than her time at the national trials.

She carried those scars with her until she exorcised them with a spectacular victory at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre, winning her first international gold medal and thanking the crowd for getting her to the wall 0.12 of a second ahead of Aimee Canny.

Angharad Evans said the Tollcross crowd carried her for the final 10 metres. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"Scotland was there to witness that and that was a very, very special moment for me," she said.

"I thanked them because leading into competitions it's so easy for doubts and negative thoughts to play a part in my mindset leading up, and I walk out and they just really uplift me and give me the confidence I need and boost me up.

"They often talk about how proud they are of us bringing back gold medals and PBs, but I'm immensely proud to have the Tartan Army supporting me in the crowd.

"Wearing the blue and white, hearing the crowd, being part of Scotland just carries you to the end. I don't think I would have had the strength and the courage I did in the last 10 metres if I wasn't in the blue and white and didn't have that crowd behind me.

"They absolutely helped me get to the end and finish in first place. So it's a medal for me but it's also a medal for Scotland."

All that from an English-born 23-year-old who is still learning the words to that famous Scottish anthem.

World.title: Quick hits: Davies makes history, Diamonds clap back in uni debate
World.content:
Rose Davies runs a "race of a lifetime" to make Australian history, and the Diamonds remain in the spotlight even off the court.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Davies makes history on the track

Rose Davies celebrated Australia's first athletics gold of the Games. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

The eagerly anticipated athletics program finally got underway on the fourth day of competition in Glasgow, and it wasn't long before Australia claimed its first gold on the track.

Rose Davies sat back for much of the women's 10,000m but timed her move to perfection, waiting until less than a kilometre remained before galloping ahead of Kenya's Diana Wanza.

And Davies eventually won in a canter, crossing the finish line almost 11 seconds before silver medallist Wanza.

Australian commentary great Bruce McAvaney called it "the race of a lifetime" during the Network Seven broadcast.

Davies became the first Australian woman to win the 10,000m at a Commonwealth Games.

"These moments come once in a lifetime, and I'm so happy I got to achieve this," Davies told the Seven Network.

2. From a cancer diagnosis to a Games final

Archie Goodburn did not win a medal but won the respect of everyone as he competes while dealing with brain tumours. (Getty Images: SNS Group/Ross MacDonald)

When people say the phrase "there are more important things in life than sport" they're probably speaking about Scotland's Archie Goodburn.

The 25-year-old breaststroke specialist had a chance to compete at the Paris Olympics when he was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours in 2024.

But speaking after his race in the final, where he finished seventh, his interview put everything in perspective and made it very hard not to get emotional watching him.

"My dream was to make the final. But outside the pool I dream, like, of a future where brain cancer isn't the biggest killer of those under 40," he said.

"[A dream] where the UK government establish a national brain cancer lead to make that change, and I'd much prefer that that change was made and that dream is completed than any of my personal goals in the pool.

"Because what families and young people are going through out there is really beyond the comprehension of many people out here and certainly far harder than anything I've ever had to do as a world-class sportsman."

3. Welsh sisters twinning in bronze

Seeing double? (Getty Images: PA Images/Owen Humphreys)

Wales has not been flush with supreme gymnasts at the Commonwealth Games.

But given their national colour, perhaps it's no surprise that at these Scottish Games that two have come along at once, like lithe, smiling versions of red London buses.

Both Abi Roper and Emily Roper were in action in the vault, with Abi claiming a bronze medal with a score of 13.433, just a fraction ahead of her identical twin sister who scored 13.283 after being penalised 0.3 for her landing on her second vault.

Then, an hour or so later, Emily put her disappointment behind her to deliver a display worthy of a medal, also winning bronze behind Australian gold medal winner Katie McDonald.

In a heartening display of sisterly love, Abi could be seen roaring her support from the stands, her own bronze medal dangling around her neck, as her sister delivered the performance of her life to win Wales its first-ever medal on that apparatus at a Commonwealth Games.

"Sometimes we bicker because we are competitive, so we are constantly fighting to see who is better," Emily told a BBC interviewer in 2025.

Who knows how much bickering there would have been had Emily come away from Glasgow empty-handed.

4. Diamonds can't help being icons, even on a day off

After winning their first two matches, our netball world champions had day four off in Glasgow. But everyone's still talking about the Diamonds: just not for the broadcast-related reason you might expect.

Diamonds disappointed first two games only live on streaming service Diamonds fans are disappointed to discover Australia's dominant netball team's Glasgow matches are only being aired live on Seven's online streaming service.

Folks online have been debating Australia's netball uniform, which rides up during play and often ends up looking more like a singlet.

Some are worried the poor design is distracting our goal shooters, who have to take their shots before readjusting the awkward uniform (lest they be penalised for a held ball!).

Currently competing in her third Commonwealth Games, Courtney Bruce has worn a few iterations of the kit over the years, and she says the team isn't too worried about the 2026 uniform.

"It is what it is, there's literally nothing we can do about it, [so] we don't think about it," she told the ABC.

In a video posted on social media Commonwealth Games debutant Sophie Garbin poked fun at what she described as "the most talked about" aspect of the Glasgow event.

Loading...

All it takes is one look at the comment section to see people on either side of the heated debate: from supporters saying shorter dresses are easier to play in, to those who reckon the Diamonds look "silly".

Responding to haters, Bruce says it's a "good thing we're strong … fit, and we train hard".

I mean, it's not like they aren't wearing shorts under the dress. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

5. Mollie O'Callaghan pulls out of the backstroke

Mollie O'Callaghan has withdrawn from the 50m backstroke. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Coming into this Commonwealth Games, Mollie O'Callaghan revealed she was managing a back injury, and it cost her a chance in her backup event the 50m backstroke.

The 22-year-old was worried that she might not even be able to compete in Glasgow after scans revealed stress fractures and bone bruising on her lumbar spine.

She was, however, cleared by a specialist to compete.

"Things might look a little different for me at the Commonwealth Games and Pan Pacs, but I'll give everything I have and do my absolute best every time I race," O'Callaghan said in an Instagram post before the Games.

Some things remained the same though, the Queenslander claiming yet another gold medal for her burgeoning collection in the 200m freestyle and 4x100m freestyle relay.

However, she withdrew from the mixed 4x100m freestyle relay and did not line up in the 50m backstroke heats on Monday morning to focus on the 100m freestyle final that evening.

World.title: Sabalenka, Djokovic lead mixed doubles teams for US Open
World.content:
Top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka and 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic headline the initial list of 16 teams entered into the US Open mixed doubles championship.

The tournament was overhauled last year, with a $US1 million ($1.43 million) prize going to the winners, in an effort to get top singles players to compete. Many of those types of stars were listed among the teams announced Monday by the US Tennis Association.

Iga Świątek and Casper Ruud, the runners-up in 2025, are entered again, along with Elena Rybakina and Taylor Fritz, the Japanese duo of Naomi Osaka and Kei Nishikori, along with Jessica Pegula and Jack Draper.

The main draw will be played over two days on August 25-26, with all the matches set to be held in Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium, the two biggest venues at the US Open.

Teams can enter up until August 17, when the six duos with the best combined singles rankings at the time will be automatically entered into the main draw.

That means Sabalenka, the two-time defending US Open women's champion and Djokovic, still ranked number five on the men's tour at age 39, will be safely into the field.

Eight teams will be given wild cards by the USTA, and two other teams will play their way into the field through a qualifying tournament to be held from August 24.

Defending champions win US Open mixed doubles final Italian pair Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori accomplish their "mission" by winning the US Open mixed doubles title for the second straight year in a controversially revamped format.

The remainder of the teams that were entered as of Monday:

Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev; Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli; Diana Shnaider and Daniil Medvedev; Amanda Anisimova and Learner Tien; Alex Eala and Felix Auger-Aliassime; Leylah Fernandez and Frances Tiafoe; Taylor Townsend and Alexander Zverev; Elena-Gabriela Ruse and Nuno Borges; Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori; Katerina Siniakova and Henry Patten; and siblings Peyton Stearns and Preston Stearns.

Errani and Vavassori are the two-time defending US Open champions. The Italians needed a wild card to get into last year's event because their singles ranking was too low, and that will be the case again this year.

The US Open was initially criticised last year because the format of the event shut out doubles specialists such as Errani and Vavassori, but the tournament certainly seemed a success, helping draw 78,000 fans to the grounds and selling out Ashe both days.

"Any time you can bring women and men together on the same team, you showcase tennis at its best. This is exactly what the mixed doubles championship does," USTA CEO Craig Tiley said in a statement.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"The mixed doubles championship is an innovation that will engage new audiences and give our fans another opportunity to see the biggest stars compete together."

Errani and Vavassori were the only traditional doubles team in last year's tournament.

There is a chance for more this year — Siniakova and Patten are doubles specialists — with the addition of the eight-team qualifying tournament, which will include six direct entries and two wild cards.

The format will be best-of-three-set matches with sets to four games, tiebreakers at 4-all and a 10-point match tie-break instead of a third set, through the semifinals. The final will be standard scoring with sets to six games and a tiebreaker at 6-all, and a 10-point match tiebreaker if necessary.

World.title: 'A gorgeous human' gets her solo moment and still shares it with her mates
World.content:
There aren't many legacies in sport as dominant as Australia in the women's 4x100m freestyle relay.

The first night of the Glasgow program marked the team's 19th victory in the past 21 major international finals across the Olympics, long-course world championships, Pan Pacs and Commonwealth Games.

It also marked the sixth time Meg Harris had stood on the top step of the podium with her teammates in those events, bridging the gap from the Campbells era to these Commonwealth Games and onwards towards Brisbane 2032.

But on Tuesday morning (AEST), when Mollie O'Callaghan and Shayna Jack joined her up there, they did so with her blessing, of course, after she became the solo 100m champion for the first time.

Meg Harris (centre) pipped superstars Shayna Jack (left) and Mollie O'Callaghan to the wall. (Gety Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

"It's pretty incredible, I've never done that before. I've never been in that position," Harris said.

"Hopefully this is just the start of my journey. I'm pretty happy with that. These girls are absolutely incredible, so any chance I get to stand on the podium with them is great."

The trials in June marked the first time she had made the team as an individual 100m swimmer.

Glasgow 2026 day four live Australia wins nine gold medals across the pool, athletics track and in the gymnastics on day four in Glasgow.

The 24-year-old admitted to struggling with motivation in the 100m after the Paris Olympics, rediscovering her love for the sport through her pet 50m event, where she won the world title in Singapore last year.

"I've always loved the [100m] race," she said.

"The 50m was something I've always loved and always known I've enjoyed racing that … but the 100m is always the one I've been working towards in the long run. I guess I need to take a step back and enjoy it for a while."

Harris's win was one of seven gold medals on the night for Australia, with Alex Perkins in the 100m butterfly and Jenna Forrester in the 400m individual medley also enjoying a breakout meet.

Jenna Forrester has enjoyed a breakout Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Forrester's victory added to her surprise 200m backstroke victory three nights earlier.

"We all really get around each other, and that's what makes Team Australia really special and successful," Perkins said.

Little did she know how true that was.

Minutes earlier, Harris had made an immediate pivot from star performer to cheer captain, stepping away from her media obligations to cheer Perkins on with every stroke as she powered to victory.

"She's amazing; all those girls are in the 100m freestyle," Perkins said.

"[They're] so successful in that event and [Harris is] just also a gorgeous human. I was really proud; it was really inspiring to watch her before my event."

100m butterfly gold medallist Alex Perkins is a big fan of Meg Harris. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Perkins and Harris are kindred spirits, two swimmers winning their favourite events for the first time after years of toil while in their mid-20s (Perkins celebrating gold on her 26th birthday).

Along with Forrester, Sam Short, Lani Pallister and a slew of other gold medallists on the night and at these Games, it's all part of a moment of transition for the Dolphins in Glasgow.

It's not so much a passing of the baton as simply getting more hands on it.

"We've got a home [Olympic] Games in 2032, we're all trying to do our best and make the most of every moment," Perkins said.

And Harris is a key part of that.

The 4x100m freestyle squad featured eight swimmers in Glasgow: Brittany Castelluzzo (25), Inez Miller (19), Jessica Cole (19) and Hannah Casey (20) in their heat; and Harris, Perkins, Jack and O'Callaghan in the final.

The jewel in Australian swimming's crown is central to the rejuvenation that never really stops for this all-conquering team.

In among the Dolphins, they call themselves "the starfish", according to the retiring Jack.

Swimming is perhaps the loneliest of all elite sport pursuits, so finding that connection is crucial to, if you'll pardon the pun, keeping your head above water.

"Meg's my roommate here, which I'm really grateful for because we do have a lot of events together and being able to share in those moments with her is extremely special to me," Jack said.

"Swimming is such an event that can be quite isolating. That's also why I love the relays because you get to share in those special moments with somebody else, and being able to go 1-2-3 tonight, it's just another moment I get to share with these amazing girls."
